The **Open Entrance to the King’s Palace** <note>original: "Introitū Regis Palatij," referring to the famous alchemical work *Introitus Apertus ad Occlusum Regis Palatium* by Eirenaeus Philalethes.</note> has been preserved as a fine manuscript for two years, along with some other excellent little treatises and the **Reformation of the Bohemians** <note>original: "Reform. d. I ask the same concerning the time and the person of the author himself, from whom three labored treatises have come forth: 1. **Methodical Instruction**, being an emended manuscript of **Geber** <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–c. 815), a foundational figure in alchemy whose works were central to European laboratory practice.</note>; 2. **A Short Introduction to the Head of Wisdom** <note>original: "brevia Manuductio ad Cap. Sophiæ."</note>; and 3. **Experienced and Speculative Philosophy**. I have learned of these alone through <unclear>...</unclear>. Others also received a very large [report] from "The Horse" <note>original: "dem Roß." ---

Accordingly, "The Horse" wished to be informed by me that before the Lords of the Crown, at a time when an Englishman named **George Starkey** <note>George Starkey (1628–1665) was an American-born physician and alchemist who is widely believed to be the man behind the pseudonym Eirenaeus Philalethes.</note> left a fine manuscript in Rome, in which such treatises were written as: 1. **A Brief Introduction to the Ruby Artifice** <note>original: "Brevis manuductio ad Rubiñ artific." This refers to the "Ruby" or the Red Stone, the final stage of the Great Work.</note> (as found in that manuscript); 2. **The Fountain of Chemical Truth**; and 3. **The Open Entrance**, etc. This came with the report that he obtained them from someone who was staying there, devoted to labor and study according to the [way of the] **Adepts** <note>An "Adept" is an alchemist who has successfully discovered the Philosopher's Stone.</note>. He is said to have brought these with him from there; this "Adept" knowledge was a foundation of the art and held great weight for **Starkey**. Additionally, something of the White <unclear>...</unclear> <note>Likely the "White Stone" or "White Tincture," which transmutes base metals into silver.</note> was secretly communicated to him. This is his further report.

## 6.
# Concerning the Fire.

Because the Work is Divine, the fire <note>represented by the symbol $\triangle$</note> must also be such a thing; and not a single spark of artificial fire is added to the <term>Coagulation</term> <note>the process of thickening or solidifying a liquid substance</note>.

## 7.
# Concerning the Colors.

The <term>Matter</term> <note>original: "Materia"; the base substance used in the alchemical process</note> is at first coal-black; afterwards it becomes sky-blue, then snow-white, then finally golden-yellow, but ultimately red like a ruby.

## 8.
# Concerning its Form.

To speak of its form, it is a fatty, oily being once it has become ruby-red, yet of a dry <term>Substance</term>. It shines upon its surface like precious stones; it breathes out blue, golden-yellow, fiery, and snow-white shining transparent parts like <term>Selenite</term> <note>original: "Marien-Glaß"; literally "Mary's Glass," a transparent gypsum used in reliquaries and as a glass substitute</note>, and like pure transparent gold, silver, and gemstones.

## 9.
# Its Smell.

Is on the one hand the most hideous, like that of a carcass; on the other hand, it is again very lovely and sweet, like <term>Marzipan</term> <note>an almond confection; here used to describe a surprisingly pleasant, sweet scent</note>.

# On the Transmutation of Metals.
## Chapter I.
### Concerning the Right of the Art, its Investigators, and in what Manner one may attain to this Secret.

Although people of every kind, rank, and fortune apply themselves to a certain profession, science, or art and devote their time to it, making it their highest priority to become as practiced and experienced in such an art as possible and to reach its highest level:

Nevertheless, very few are found who are particularly favored by fortune in this regard. # The First Chapter

No one should complain as if they had labored in vain, even if every mathematician <note>original: "Meßkünstler"</note> does not equal **Archimedes**, every poet does not equal **Homer**, and every orator does not equal **Cicero**. Rather, even the lesser orators, according to the **talent** <note>original: "talent," referring to the biblical parable of the talents or innate ability</note> they have received, can be useful to the common good. Indeed, all people—even if they do not achieve such great perfection or experience in the art to which they have applied themselves—may nevertheless create use and benefit within the community in which they find themselves.

But all those who apply themselves to the **transformation of metals** <note>The alchemical process of transmutation, usually turning base metals into gold</note> appear as if they labor in such a highly useful matter not only quite uselessly, but also without any understanding. For the highest step of this art is the masterpiece itself; if one can actually make and demonstrate it, then he has hit the mark. But where one does not reach that far, he has no other benefit to hope for, because the unfinished science of **Alchemy** can bring or give nothing else but vain loss of the expended costs and time. Furthermore, such a person must allow himself to be mocked and laughed at by the haters of the **Chemical Art**. However, the object <note>original: "Objectum"</note> of the art is so noble, and promises the possessor of the same such unspeakable wealth and most complete health, that almost every simple fool, as soon as he hears but a little of such an art, lets his mouth water for it; in short, he applies himself to it and takes on the name of an **Alchemist**. # The First Chapter

One finds, therefore, that the world has been so filled with such sophistical matters <note>sophistical: deceptive or fallacious arguments intended to mislead</note> that almost every beginning student of the Art is led astray by them. Conversely, nearly every scorner of the Art takes occasion from this to oppose these things with all their might. Thus, the Art itself, as well as its sincere followers, must suffer without cause, merely because of the malice of certain loose deceivers. Although these men are as ignorant in such Art as a block of wood, they nevertheless write in such a way as if they were true *Adepts* <note>original: "Adepti" – those who have attained the ultimate secrets of alchemy</note> or possessors of the Art. They freely send their deceptions into the world, so that a beginner in the Chemical Art finds therein his very first maze or labyrinth, from which there is no help for him, as he does not know how to distinguish the good books from the false ones. From these false books, the deceivers construct almost as impressive a structure as the true artists; indeed, for the most part, they promise much greater things, of which Count *Bernhard of Treviso* <note>A famous 15th-century Italian alchemist known for his long search for the Philosopher's Stone</note>—who was not inexperienced in such deceptions—writes thus:

> Unless you flee these people as you would the plague itself, you will never attain anything good in this Art.

And I have, therefore, written this treatise for the purpose of better instructing the ignorant in this science, so that they may not be miserably led astray on wandering paths. I have thus resolved, first and foremost, to defend the Art against its slanders; afterwards, I will report how those who strive after it must be qualified and disposed. Indeed, even gold and silver themselves, as well as copper—whose virtues I shall not easily describe, and whose transformation into all metals I have seen, performed, and hold in my knowledge—and that such a thing is true, all <term>Adepts</term> <note>Adepti: those who have mastered the "Great Work" of alchemy</note> or possessors of the art testify alongside me. I will tell you (if you are able to grasp it): it is called "Steel" by the author of the treatise titled *The New Chemical Light* <note>original: "novum lumen chymicum," a famous 17th-century alchemical text by Michael Sendivogius</note>, and it is the true beginning of the Work and the authentic key (provided one knows how to handle it) with which to unlock the most hidden secrets of the philosophers. 

But what can one make of the fact that the philosophers have hidden all of this, and have presented the truth to the "children of the art" <note>a traditional term for students of alchemy</note> in the form of parables under the mask of falsehood? Should the Divine Science be held in low esteem for that reason? Far be it from that. It is evident from this that there is no hindrance in the nature of the imperfect that prevents it from being transformed into something perfect; indeed, by its own nature, it is inclined to accept perfection, provided that one undertakes to perform this through a <term>homogeneous agent</term> <note>original: "agens homogeneum"; a substance of the same nature as the metal being worked upon</note> or an acting essence entirely in harmony with it, which possesses a digesting power. 

Let us, therefore, make it our concern to investigate the virtue of this thing: and first of all, we wish to present that through which it must happen, and afterwards also cite several philosophical reasons regarding it.

Concerning the first point, we say and confess that it is nothing other than gold which has been ripened to the highest degree (as far as it can be brought through nature and art), which then is no

# The Second Chapter

It may seem difficult to an inexperienced person when he reads their books, because they write so darkly, enigmatically, metaphorically, and figuratively; in part, they also mix in many false things to confuse the unworthy and the incautious, so that in such a manner they might distinguish the philosophers or the wise from the unwise. In their main objective, however, they all agree with one another and lead to the same end. Whatever they present obscurely, they do so for no other purpose than to exclude the unworthy, as they frequently testify in their books. 

However, *Bernard of Treviso* <note>original: "Bernhardus Trevisanus," a 15th-century Italian count and famous alchemist</note> (whom I hold in exceedingly high regard) is found to be very open-hearted in this art; likewise also *Ripley* the Englishman; *Flamel* the Frenchman; *Sendivogius*, author of the book *The New Light* <note>original: "Novi luminis"</note>; as well as the unnamed author of the book *The Hermetic Secret* <note>original: "Arcani Hermetici"</note>, whose name has nevertheless become known through a double anagram or transposition of letters, namely: *My hope is in the lamb* <note>original: "Spes mea in agno," an anagram for Jean d'Espagnet</note>, appearing in the book whose title is: *Handbook of Restored Physics* <note>original: "Enchiridion Physicæ restitutæ"</note>, and: *The wave of the Tagus is in our power* <note>original: "Penes nos unda Tagi," another anagram for Jean d'Espagnet</note>, which he placed in his *Hermetic Secret*. 

In this regard, I should not overlook the book: *The Ladder of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Scala Philosophorum"</note>, the great *Rose Garden* <note>original: "Rosarium"</note>, the books of *Arnold* <note>likely Arnold of Villanova</note>, the book *Children's Play* <note>original: "Ludus Puerorum"</note>, the little book of *Denis Zachaire* <note>original: "Dionysii Zacharii"</note>, *Giles de Vadis* <note>original: "Ægidium de Vadis"</note>, the writings of *Morienus*, the poetic writings of *Augurellus* concerning the art of gold-making <note>original: "Gold-Kunst," referring to alchemy</note>. Likewise also the five treatises of the small *Rose Garden*. The writings of *Pietro Bono of Ferrara* <note>original: "Petri Boni Ferrariensis"</note>; in a word, all books which agree with those mentioned should, in my opinion, be included, but where the opposite is found, they should be excluded.

# On the Transformation of Metals

<note>original: "Von Verwandlung der Metallen"</note>

When such books are placed into the hands of the student learning the Art, he must, before beginning the work, first learn to recognize the life, realm, quality, and nature of the metals, and likewise of the minerals. He should not be satisfied with knowing such things only superficially, but rather with true science <note>The author uses "Wissenschafft" here to mean systematic, proven knowledge</note>—that is, through manual practice and exercise. For this, a profound contemplation and reflection is necessary, so that he may learn to recognize and understand the origin of natural things in general <note>original: "in genere"</note>, and specifically <note>original: "in specie"</note> of mineral matters. As for myself, I intend to mention the metallic doctrine here only briefly, namely as much as is necessary for the explanation of the Art of Transformation. I diligently bypass the origin of natural things in general, contenting myself to speak only of what is sufficient for the intended purpose; nevertheless, I will touch upon the rest in an orderly and brief manner.

Now, all common philosophers have established four elements <note>The classical elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire</note> from which all things were originally composed or put together, of which all things consist, and into which they are again dissolved, and from whose various combinations different things arise. Almost all chemical philosophers <note>term: Chymische Philosophen (Alchemists who sought to understand nature through laboratory work)</note> have agreed with this unfortunate opinion. I can guess no other reason for this than that they, having their own affairs in mind, wished to proceed quickly without mature deliberation, and thus described these as the first foundations <note>original: "Fundamenta"</note> of all things. ## Chapter III.

### Concerning Gold and Silver / how they originate from a mercurial matter / and concerning the possibility of changing the imperfect metals into the perfection of the aforementioned.

From the previously mentioned fountain <note>The "fountain" refers to the *materia prima* or the primordial substance from which all metals are thought to grow.</note> is born, as has been thought, the Sun <note>The Sun is the alchemical symbol for Gold.</note> and her sister the Moon <note>The Moon is the alchemical symbol for Silver.</note>; specifically when this matter has been brought to perfection through digestion <term>digestion: a process of slow, consistent heating to mature a substance</term> or ripening. Furthermore, perfection is of two kinds: namely, either a beginning perfection or a completed one; that is, one that happens in part, and the other which happens entirely. 

Completed perfection is the highest goal toward which Nature herself aims, namely where all rawness may be boiled away, and all impurity cleansed, so that only the pure metallic nature, without any filth, triumphs in its coagulation <term>coagulation: the process of a liquid substance becoming solid or fixed</term>. Here, our Sun has its rising, and illuminates the earth with its brilliance and shine. 

The "beginning perfection," however (so to speak), is actually no true perfection; yet, in consideration of something that is imperfect in its form, it cannot improperly be called a perfection. For a formal imperfection can be judged to exist when that rawness <note>original: "crudität"</note>—which accidentally clung to the pure substance during its generation—is not boiled away, nor the foreign superfluity cleansed out, but rather remains mixed with the pure substance in such quantity during coagulation that it holds the upper hand and finally prevails: as is the case with all...

# The Third Chapter

Since the <term>Arcanum</term> <note>A secret, powerful substance or "Great Work" in alchemy.</note> is a spiritual, homogeneous substance, it enters into such imperfect metals *per minima* <note>original: "per minima" — through the smallest possible parts or atoms.</note>, or through the very smallest particles. Whatever it finds that is like itself, it seizes and protects through its overwhelming power from the violence of the burning fire, holding it fast through its more-than-perfect <term>fixity</term> <note>The ability of a substance to remain unaffected by fire or heat.</note>. Meanwhile, the burning <term>Vulcan</term> <note>The Roman god of fire, used here as a metaphor for the alchemical furnace.</note> likewise consumes the combustible elements with his flaming heat. Once these have been consumed by the fire, there remains the pure gold or silver (according to the quality of the Medicine) which withstands all the violence of the fire and passes every test. It in no way yields to that gold which comes out of the earth, but rather surpasses it.

And so we do not claim (as some unworthy slanderers reproach us) to "make" gold or silver, but rather to find and bring to pass such an *agens* <note>An active agent or catalyst.</note> which, when cast upon the imperfect metals, can permeate their smallest parts because of its homogeneity—or "one-ness of being"—and its spiritual nature. Furthermore, so that it may protect the pure substance from being consumed by the fire through its overwhelming strength and virtue, it holds onto that which it finds similar to itself until the superfluous <term>feces</term> <note>Dross, impurities, or waste matter left after a process.</note> are destroyed by the burning intensity of the fire. This operation is the gold-making transformation. All of this is performed by our secret <term>Elixir</term>, and it has, in addition, this effect: that it imparts both color and constancy to the imperfect, insofar as the Elixir itself is a partaker of the highest excellence in both

->color and fixity.<-

## Chapter IV.

# On the Seed of Gold / and whether the other metals also possess a seed / which is a debated question.

In order to preserve, propagate, and multiply every species, a seed has been ordained for all things by the Great Creator. The seed is the perfection of every thing, and whatever lacks a seed is rightly to be considered imperfect. Therefore, it is not to be doubted that a metallic seed also exists. For all metals that are now in the world, and have been until now, must either have been created within the first six days <note>A reference to the Biblical creation narrative in Genesis.</note>, or else must have subsequently grown and increased gradually. The first possibility is denied by both reason and experience. If, then, the latter is true, no one can deny that a metallic seed must exist; if this is admitted, then certainly the metal will not lose that seed during its <term>coagulation</term> <note>The process by which a liquid or vaporous substance hardens into a solid metallic form.</note>. For coagulation is an effect or an accomplished work of perfection (or rather of <term>ripening</term> <note>original: "Zeitigung" — the natural process of maturing toward a final state</note>, which leads directly to perfection, provided that external things are properly arranged). The sign of perfection, however, is the seed of that which is thus ripened; and it is therefore not to be presumed that the seed should be lost in the coagulation, but rather that it should become even nobler. Through this, it becomes clear that a metallic seed is present in the metals. It remains to be asked, however, whether

It lacks nothing except mere ripening <note>original: "Zeitigung"; the alchemical process of maturation over time within the earth.</note>, which simultaneously separates the dross <note>original: "feces"; the impurities or waste matter</note>, consumes the rawness <note>original: "crudität"</note>, and introduces fixity <note>original: "fixität"; the ability of a substance to withstand fire without evaporating</note> or stability. 

The form of gold, however, is substantial—that is, grounded upon the substance of the purified matter itself. In mature gold, however, this very same seed is most closely enclosed and triumphs in perfection.

It then becomes entirely of one form or heavenly power, so that it is suited to communicate this virtue to others—namely, to those which are related to it by the oneness of their <term>matter</term>.

# On the Transformation of Metals

The aforementioned effects are, in fact, diametrically opposed to the Work. If one observes this correctly, the frustration inherent in the Work will be easily understood: since gold—which among all bodies is the most *compact*, most *fixed* <note>original: "fixeste"; referring to a substance's ability to withstand fire without evaporating</note>, and of the strongest composition, being the most stable in fire and in no way subject to *corruption* <note>original: "corruption"; decay or chemical breakdown</note>—does not easily transition into a nature so greatly opposed to its own. Therefore, if one were to attempt to do this by force, he would achieve nothing. For this reason, an *agent* <note>original: "agens"; the active force or substance that triggers a change</note> of overwhelming power is required for this to happen. This *agent* must be homogeneous or of one essence <note>original: "einwesig"</note>, as well as of close friendship and spiritual in nature, so that it is related to the body yet can nevertheless overcome it and penetrate to its innermost core. By this means, the very interior of the gold is opened and dissolved to such an extent that not even the smallest part remains true, common gold. Thus, this must necessarily be no common *agent*: for gold will not so easily cast off its form, but will rather resist and struggle for as long as possible until it is finally overcome, succumbs, and dies. That our *agent* must also be endowed with the power to bring to life follows from the fact that it can awaken a new, pure body from dead remains.

### Concerning the Philosophical first-acting Essence called the *first agent* <note>original: "agens primum"</note> / or concerning the Mother / into which our seed must be released / and also therein be brought to maturity.

However, even this is not yet enough; rather, it must also stand in contrariety or opposition to gold in all its qualities, by which it differs or is distinguished from the water (wherein the seed lies). Just as the former <note>gold</note> is highly fixed and stable, the latter <note>the secret water</note> is exceedingly volatile. The former is a most dense and compact body, the latter an immeasurably penetrating spirit; the former thick, the latter subtle; the former dead, the latter living and life-giving. Therefore, it must be concluded that <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurius"; here referring to the "Philosophical Mercury," not common quicksilver</note> alone is the true key to the <term>Chymical Art</term> <note>Alchemy</note>, which in truth is that same "dry water" of which the <term>Philosophers</term> <note>the ancient alchemical authorities</note> so often speak; which flows and runs, and yet does not wet the hands of him who touches it, nor anything else that is not of the unity of its own matter. And not only this, but it is furthermore endowed with all the virtues previously recounted. This is our Gatekeeper, our Balsam, Oil, Honey, our Urine, May-dew, Female, Mother, Egg, secret Furnace, Hearth, Sieve, Marble-stone, true Fire, poisonous Dragon, our <term>Theriac</term> <note>a universal antidote or panacea</note>, Spirits of Wine, Green Lion, Hermetic Bird, Hermogenes' Goose, the two-edged sword in the hand of the Cherub who guards the way to the Tree of Life, and countless other names besides by which it is called. It is our true secret vessel, as well as the Philosophical Garden wherein our Sun rises and is resurrected. It is the royal, mineral, and triumphant, vegetative <term>Lead-Flower</term> <note>original: "Bley-Blume"; likely referring to the "Flower of Saturn" or a purified state of lead ore</note>.

They do not comprehend the philosophical Mercury <note>original: "Mercurii"</note> in its underlying causes, and therefore, in their uncertainty, they believe that something else must be chosen in place of common mercury. However, they do not know in what way common mercury is deficient, or why it cannot be the true Mercury of the Sages. # The Eighth Chapter

Chemists <note>original: "Chymisten"; here referring to alchemists and early chemical philosophers</note> note as an absolute certainty that no other Mercury <note>The "Mercury of the Philosophers," believed to be the essential fluid component of all metals</note> from which all metals are found exists, other than the common kind (in respect to its origin). This substance, after it has been generated in the veins of the earth, is entirely destined or ordained for the birthing of a metal, so long as it remains in a place suitable and fit for generation and is kept free from the raw air. It retains within itself a movement and impulse that incites it toward a perfect generation. 

However, if the suitability of the place is violated or damaged by some accident, this material is immediately struck, as if by the hammer of death. It loses all movement entirely and can be brought no further. It is no different than an egg upon which a brooding hen has sat for a time, which is rendered unfit to bring forth any fruit by the onset of cold. In such a case, the life or the altering internal warmth vanishes due to the lack of external heat. That which was previously progressing daily toward perfection, having been hindered by the preceding accident, becomes a deformity <note>original: "Mißgeburt"; a "misbirth" or failed creation</note>, and no hope remains for any future movement to occur of its own accord. 

And this is therefore the reason why various people, who have attempted to ripen such Mercury above the earth through devised artificial heat, have carried away a reward for their work that was not at all worth the effort. # On the Transformation of Metals

Everything is merely disposed appropriately from the outside, and in such a manner leaves behind in things an impression or imprinting of itself. When this is accepted by the things, it brings forth a ferment <note>A substance that causes fermentation or chemical change, often used in alchemy to describe the "yeast" of the Great Work.</note>, which is the true author or instigator of all transformation. Through its own ferment-like scent, it incites the things in which it dwells toward a movement that is both destructive and generative.

However, as soon as those external circumstances required for this process are lacking, everything comes to a standstill; such a ruin cannot then be easily repaired by any art. We are then left with a raw, metallic, untimely, cold material that has not been purified by boiling. In the context of minerals, this material emulates the nature of something common, and in the context of vegetables and animals, it mimics the nature of well-water or rainwater.

This, therefore, is the true matter of the *Philosophical Mercury* <note>original: "Mercurii Philosophici"; the essential "First Matter" of the alchemists, not to be confused with common quicksilver.</note>, and it lacks only the form of the same, for which it must exchange its own so that what we seek may arise from it. Two defects or deficiencies primarily keep it distant from this form: first, a *superfluity* <note>original: "superfluität"</note> or excess which it carries with it; and second, a deficiency—namely, of spiritual virtue.

The superfluity is also of two kinds: namely, an earthly one or "leprosy," and a watery one or "dropsy" <note>The author uses medical terms for skin disease and fluid retention to describe impurities in the metal.</note>. The deficiency, however, consists in this: that there is in it a lack of warmth, of the true Sulfur <note>original: "Schwefels"; in alchemy, Sulfur represents the active, masculine, and combustible principle.</note>, the addition or replacement of which will purge all superfluity from it. For the philosophical water is, as it were, a female mother; yet no mother can be fit for generation <note>The act of producing or bringing into being.</note> without warmth.

# Chapter 8: On the Transformation of Metals

Therefore, apply yourself to the task and fulfill in the *Mercury* <note>The "Mercury of the Philosophers," a specialized substance believed to be the root of all metals, not common quicksilver.</note> what it lacks; namely, the fiery power to burn. In doing so, all the *dross* <note>original: "feces"; the impurities or waste matter in a substance</note> will fall away from the *Mercury* of its own accord, which you must separate with the greatest precision. If you do this, you will have conducted yourself as befits an exceedingly wise and experienced *Philosopher*. At that point, *Jupiter* <note>In alchemy, Jupiter represents the metal Tin or a specific stage of whitening/brightening in the process.</note> has taken over the reign, who, by dispersing all the *Saturnine* <note>original: "Saturnischen"; referring to Saturn, the symbol for Lead and for darkness or heaviness.</note> clouds, causes a bright, shining fountain to spring forth for you. You will marvel at the uncommon brilliance of its water, whose extraordinary powers—which it receives not from the *matter* but from the *Form* <note>In Aristotelian terms, the "Form" is the essential nature or soul of a thing that gives it its specific properties.</note>—are to be found in no other thing in the entire world.

For it *dissolves* <note>original: "solviret"</note> gold in a natural way through a true *philosophical* dissolution; not as the *Sophistic* <note>A term used by true alchemists to describe "puffers" or fraudulent chemists who used harsh, unnatural methods.</note> laborers *dissolve* it through *corrosive*, destructive waters <note>Likely referring to strong acids like Aqua Regia.</note>, and who strive as much as they can to alienate it from its metallic *matter*. This *Mercury* naturally brings forth gold and silver from within itself; it also provides the *secret* <note>original: "arcanum"</note> of drinkable gold, or *potable gold* <note>original: "auri potabilis"; a legendary medicinal elixir thought to grant longevity.</note>, which I write with full knowledge, and the masters of the art likewise know and testify to this. I wish, therefore, to conclude this little treatise herewith; for whatever remains to be said will yet be presented by me candidly in a separate writing. In the meantime, fare well, make use of this, and await the blessing from **GOD**.

## The Second Treatise.
# A Brief Guide to the Heavenly Ruby.
## Concerning the Philosopher’s Stone and its Secret.

The Philosopher’s Stone <note>original: "Stein der Weisen"</note> is a heavenly, spiritual, penetrating, and fixed substance, which perfects or completes all metals into true gold or silver (according to the quality of the Medicine <note>In alchemy, the "Medicine" refers to the elixir or tincture used to heal "sick" or base metals into "healthy" gold</note>), which withstands all tests; and this occurs through the imitation of Nature and her workings, as closely as can possibly be achieved.

The Chemical Art <note>original: "Chymische Kunst"</note> concerns itself with this substance, treating and teaching the manner and the way to accomplish this; yet this does not happen through many different things, but only through one single thing, to which nothing must be added, nor anything taken away, but from which only the superfluous must be removed.

Regarding the legitimacy of this Art, experience could best convince people in such a matter; for if it were proven by the deed itself that true gold were made through this Art, then there would be no further reason to doubt its right and utility. That all imperfect metals are transmutable <note>original: "transmutirlich"</note> or capable of being transformed in this way is evident from the fact that they are all ordained toward one end: namely, toward perfection.

# Concerning the Heavenly Ruby

Take my words and lock them deep within your heart.

You have previously heard of the possibility of <term>transmutation</term> <note>The alchemical process of changing one substance into another, specifically base metals into gold.</note> or transformation; namely, that every single thing which is destined for perfection, but has remained imperfect due to a lack of ripening, can be made perfect and brought to maturity through the <term>application</term> of such an <term>agent</term> <note>original: "agentis"; the active force or substance that triggers a change.</note>. This agent must be of the same essence and nature as the perfection for which the imperfect thing was intended, but it must possess a greater degree of perfection. It is perfected to the extent that the <term>agent</term> is <term>more than perfect</term> <note>original: "plusquamperfect"; a state of over-ripeness or concentrated power.</note> with overflowing <term>maturity</term> or ripeness and virtue. Such is the relationship between our Stone and all other imperfect metals; therefore, we consider it beyond all dispute that they are capable of being transformed by it into gold and silver.

Therefore, you lovers of wisdom, take heed of what and of what kind of nature that thing must be which can accomplish this: which has been called "the Stone" by the philosophers. However, it is in every human being and in every thing; it is also to be found at any time of the year in its place. Pay attention to these words and seal up the secrets: For it will certainly and truly consist of the elements, because nothing is more <term>universal</term> or general than they are. Yet, it does not consist of the bare and simple elements, but rather those which are mixed and stand against one another in an equal <term>ana-proportion</term> <note>original: "anatischen proportion"; likely derived from the Greek 'ana', meaning in equal parts or according to a proper ratio.</note>. That is to say, it represents every element recognizably through its own property. Therefore, our Stone is in every thing, or is every thing, or much more, is made from every thing or element.

It would be just as absurd if someone were to try and make our **Stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold.</note> from animals, herbs, and similar things. It is as if the beginning of making gold were to be sought anywhere else but in gold alone. Therefore, our Stone must not be sought in such things, as it must represent and demonstrate the natural properties of true gold—which are certainly not to be found in, nor expected from, such [organic] things. Unless, of course, we wished to create the **seeds** <note>In alchemy, "seeds" refers to the essential generative principle or "sperm" of metals believed to be implanted by nature.</note> ourselves, which belongs to **God** alone; and if anyone were to promise to do such a thing, he would be false and a liar.

Therefore, it should be enough for us to dispose, or arrange and apply, those seeds that are already prepared and present. But we should have no thoughts of wanting to create them anew from foreign things, which is altogether impossible to do. And even if it could happen, such artificial seeds could do no more than the natural ones which Nature has already prepared for our **Work**. Thus, one should in no way believe anyone who presumes to bring forth the seed of metals from herbs and similar things. For although he may strangely deceive the inexperienced under the title and name of a **Philosopher** <note>A "Philosopher" in this context refers specifically to an Alchemist or "Philosopher by Fire."</note> and experienced artist, it is easy to imagine that since he does not know how to rightly use the seeds that are already created, he will be even less able to create such seeds anew.

# Concerning the Heavenly Ruby

The **spirit** <note>original: "spiritus"</note> or **fifth essence** <note>The "quintessence," believed to be the purest element beyond the four earthly ones.</note> which, next to the rational soul, is the noblest among all creatures; it brings all diseases and all imperfections—both in **living beings** <note>original: "animalien"</note> and **metals** (according to the nature of the **medicine**)—into the most precise and perfect state of balance. And this is truly our **microcosm** <note>original: "kleine Welt" (little world); the idea that man or the Stone contains the entire universe within itself.</note> which we hold in such high regard. And once one possesses this **Stone** or **powder** or **quintessence**, then hereafter, by Divine help, there shall be no lack of wealth and health; to Him be honor in eternity.

But so that I may proceed to the final part of this work I have undertaken, and show by what means one may arrive at this Stone of ours: For one must not seek it ready-made by nature, but must compose it oneself through art and deep understanding, yet through the help and cooperation of nature. For just as it has already been abundantly shown that the **matter** of this Stone must be taken from nowhere else but the metals, so nevertheless such metals are by no means our Stone. This is quite easy to understand, since they have a different form distinct from our Stone. Nevertheless, I do not deny that our matter must be extracted from them; if it is to be brought out, then the first form of the metal must necessarily be put away beforehand, and this while retaining its **species** <note>The essential "kind" or "nature" of the metal.</note> or type, even though it involves the destruction of this **particular and individual metal**. ## Concerning Calcination.

Calcination is the first purification of the Stone, a drying out of the moisture through the power of natural heat, which is excited by the external heat of the fire. In the first conjunction <note>The joining of two substances, often symbolized as a chemical marriage.</note>, our water creates a distinction between the sulfur and the mercury <note>The two primary principles of alchemy; sulfur represents the active, masculine, and combustible principle, while mercury represents the passive, feminine, and metallic principle.</note>, or between the volatile and the fixed. These are enemies to one another and are two unequal things; it is our duty, however, to bring such things to purity. But these adverse qualities are not reconciled except through a medium. Thus, in our first operation, there are four adverse qualities: namely Heat, Cold, Dryness, and Moisture. Among these, two—heat and dryness—are attributed to the sulfur, while cold and moisture are assigned to the mercury. They are thus diametrically opposed to one another: the heat of the sulfur against the cold of the mercury, and likewise the moisture of the mercury against the dryness of the sulfur. We must now harmonize such adversities, which cannot happen without a medium; the medium, however, partakes of both qualities and is suited to both. For example, if we wished to harmonize heat and cold with one another, the medium through which this can happen is dryness, because it can be added and joined to both—namely to heat as well as to cold. # Of the Heavenly Ruby.

The <term>calcination</term><note>The process of reducing a solid to a powder through heat; in alchemy, it often refers to the "death" or purification of the material.</note> has now taken place. For as soon as the warmth begins to work, the cold and moist elements cannot endure it and therefore rise to the height, gather there in drops, and fall back down, bringing as much as possible into its own likeness. This continues until finally everything is resolved together into a kind of fatty and <term>glutinous</term><note>Sticky or viscous, indicating the "mercurial" state of the matter.</note> water. In this manner, our labors are linked together like a chain, so that one is always the cause and beginning of the other, and none can be held or understood without the rest.

However, in order to instruct the sons of art more thoroughly, and to keep the unworthy as far as possible from this art, we treat or present various effects as if they were separate, even though there is nothing more than a single recipe, one thing, one governance, and an orderly, successive disposition toward the **Blackness**, **Whiteness**, and **Redness** <note>The three main stages of the Great Work: Nigredo, Albedo, and Rubedo.</note>. We wish to be understood in no other way than this; and therefore, every person who wishes to be a true <term>Philosopher</term><note>A "Philosopher" in this context is a practicing alchemist seeking the hidden truths of nature.</note> must look to the sense, and not the literal letter, of those who write on this art.

But so that one may arrive at our true calcination, one must take good heed of the following things.

First, one must procure our <term>Mercury</term><note>Not common quicksilver, but the "Philosophical Mercury," the living spirit or prime matter of the stone.</note>, without which nothing can be accomplished in this art. See to it, therefore, that you are not deceived by common mercury, which is altogether useless for our art; for even if you were to work with it until Judgment Day, you would find nothing in it.

Here it might be objected that, according to the first stirring of the matter, the <term>tincture</term><note>The "tincture" refers to the active, transformative essence or soul of the material being worked upon.</note> should emerge every hour and moment, and the color of the emerging tincture is the blackest black. For although it is called the "blackest," it noticeably turns toward white. # Chemical Philosophy

Water, which in its nature is cold and moist, nevertheless—when it is mixed with any vegetable matter during the process of boiling—receives and adopts other properties from the thing with which it has been mixed. Its power and spirit, or life, which has its seat in the water, enters into the water through the boiling process, and the water adopts its nature through a process of transformation. Yet, the coarse and corporeal earthly part of the boiled substance is not the same <term>Spiritus</term> <note>The "spirit" or volatile essence of a substance</note> that changes the watery qualities; rather, it is separable from the moisture after the boiling is complete.

Exactly the same is to be understood regarding Mercury <note>original: "Mercurio"</note> and its various forms, though with some distinction. For whatever metal or mineral is so befriended by Mercury that it can be mixed and boiled with it in the smallest parts, that same Mercury adopts other qualities according to the nature of the metal mixed with it, and casts off its <term>feces</term> <note>The dregs or impure sediment left after a process</note>. In the same way, the metallic and mineral species must be boiled within it in a prepared and alternating manner; for it is their "water," into which the mineral spirits are released through boiling. They alter the Mercury in no other way than vegetables alter common water when they are boiled in it.

# Chemical Philosophy

In Mercury, the elements are homogeneous or of a single essence, and are tempered with one another in such a way that neither can be separated from the other. They are also so powerfully united that a wonderful subtlety of matter and density of substance exist together, such that the colors within are kept hidden. Therefore, if any proportion of the Mercury is corrupted—whether this happens in a destructive manner with corrosive things, or in a generative manner with its own designated body—it will immediately reveal the color incorporated into its substance.

However, the proportions of Mercury are considered in terms of Earth and Water. The latter <note>Water</note> makes it running and fluid; in consideration of the former <note>Earth</note>, it wets nothing that it touches, except only that which is of the same harmony as its own nature. Thus, from what has just been said, all the errors of those who work with Mercury are made manifest. For some destroy or divide its homogeneity by drying it out with various sublimations <note>The process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then cools back into a solid</note>; others destroy the Earth and throw it out of its proportion by introducing a transparency to it. These people, as many as they may be, never achieve anything other than a sophisticated <note>In this context, "sophistic" means fraudulent or counterfeit</note> work.

For Mercury is the sperm <note>The generative seed or life-force</note> of the metals, which Nature with great wisdom has formed into a metal within the veins of the Earth. It lacks nothing further except a pure digestion <note>A slow, steady heating process used to mature a substance</note>. It is, however, not digested or ripened by anything other than a pure metallic sulfur that does not burn, which it indeed possesses in its center. Through this sulfur, Nature would, over a long period of time, produce gold from it; but how such a thing is done through Art <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy or the intentional acceleration of natural processes</note>...

# Preface

The scarcity and frequent depletion of the aforementioned published <term>treatises</term> <note>original: "Tractaten"</note> might perhaps have enticed certain profit-seekers to make it their business to hunt for even greater gain and profit from such works. Since no further treatise is available from the <term>author</term> <note>original: "Authore"</note> himself, many a person might knowingly publish the work of another under his name. Indeed, it appears that a beginning has already been made with the present volume, and perhaps even more such <term>deceptions</term> <note>original: "Unterschleiff"</note> might follow.

For the reader, in reading through them, will very easily be able to notice that such newly-issued treatises were not composed by the previous author. This is because our true author, in his treatise titled *The Open Entrance* <note>original: "Introitus Apertus," a famous 17th-century alchemical text</note>, expressly reports that because he himself is an <term>Adept</term> <note>original: "Adeptus," one who has mastered the secret of the Philosopher's Stone</note> or a possessor of the Art, and writes more clearly than any before him, he neither needs nor wishes to make use of the testimonies and writings of other <term>philosophers</term> <note>meaning alchemists</note>, nor to introduce them into his own writings. 

Yet, in these current treatises—and especially the first one titled *An Orderly Narration*—quite the opposite appears. There, one sees almost nothing else before them but vain, patched-together sayings from other philosophers, which are also for the most part very incorrectly cited, as anyone can easily become aware of when they examine the cited...

# Preface.

I have no reason to suspect that they were intended for the press, especially those works published after his death; indeed, it remains to be seen whether he composed everything himself and is truly the <term>Author</term> <note>original: "Author"</note> of the same. Rather, it may well be that he—as most devotees of this science <note>The "science" refers to alchemy or hermetic philosophy</note> are accustomed to do—obtained or transcribed one or another <term>manuscript</term> <note>original: "manuſcripta"</note> from others and kept them among his own books and effects. Now, after his death, these are attributed to him by others as if they were his own <term>invention</term> <note>original: "invention"</note> and labor. Doubtless, it helps significantly that there is a considerable demand for anything coming from this author, and whatever is printed under the name assigned to him sells well and is readily paid for. Because it is profitable for the <term>publishers</term> <note>original: "Verlegern"</note>, they are not so precise about who the actual author might be; as long as the buyers are satisfied with it, they let it pass.

## The Medicine of the First Order.

The Medicine of the First Order is that <term>Preparation</term> <note>original: Præparation; the chemical process of making a substance ready for use</note> of the Stone which precedes the operation of the perfect <term>Preparation</term>. It is properly called the Separation of the Elements and the purification of each one of them, according to the requirements of Nature. However, the elements cannot be purified unless one first thoroughly recognizes all their natures and infirmities. For in the work of the Medicine of the First Order, there are several infirmities which arise partly from their minerals and partly from the elements themselves. # Concerning the Philosophical Stone.

This occurs, however, through the reduction or reintegration of the Moist with the Dry, proceeding immediately after their preparation. For otherwise, the Moist would not accept the Dry, nor the Spirit the Body, unless they were thoroughly washed of their impurities by the help of the separation of the elements; through calcining <note>term: Calcination; heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to powder</note>, distilling, dissolving, and congealing. And this is what Hermes, the prince of this teaching, intends to indicate when he speaks in his Emerald Tablet <note>original: "Smaragdinischen Tafel"; a foundational hermetic text</note>: **"You shall separate the earth from the fire and the subtle from the gross."** For through the separation of the elements, and through tempered or moderate digestion <note>term: Digestion; the slow heating of a substance in a sealed vessel</note> and calcination, the sulfurous combustibles are burnt away and utterly destroyed by the fire and the earth. The body is made powerfully tender and subtle through such digestion, and the waters are purified of their dross through distilling, and through subtilization are converted into the nature of air by rising in lightness.

From this it now appears that, unless the destructible matter were separated through the destruction of the Stone—by calcining and distilling, with the constant bringing back of that which is above onto that which is below—it would be impossible to purify the same. And it is therefore necessary that after the corruption <note>The stage of "putrefaction" where the matter breaks down and turns black</note> of our Stone, the compound of the Stone itself be purified of all its weaknesses following its separation through the four elements, before the Mercury <note>The "spirit" or transformative principle in alchemy</note> is joined with the body, in order to achieve such a—

# On the Philosopher's Stone.

To begin the *preparation* <note>original: "præparation"</note>, which is a creation or complete preparation of our Stone.

And for this reason, it is necessary that the Stone be divided through the four *Elements* <note>original: "Elementa"</note> by means of calcinations <note>the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile matter</note> and distillations. Such division occurs for this purpose: so that the substance of the Stone becomes pure, and the entire *composite* <note>original: "compositum"</note>, after the separation of the dross and dregs, becomes a pure *Mercury* <note>original: "Mercurius"</note>, which possesses the property of flowing and of fixing <note>becoming stable and resistant to heat</note>.

And we tell you that this *separation* of the *Elements* cannot happen without *solution* <note>dissolving the substance</note>, nor can the *solution* or dissolving happen without *putrefaction* <note>the breaking down or "rotting" of the matter</note>, which is a destruction of our Stone. Through this, the *spirit* <note>original: "spiritus"</note> is mixed with the body and its *Elements*, and it is this very process which makes them volatile, as appears in their separations. Furthermore, the aforementioned things do not properly accept one another unless they are both entirely pure beforehand; for the body does not accept the spirit, nor the *spirit* the body—so that the spiritual might become bodily and the bodily spiritual—unless they are first most perfectly healed of all weakness. But when they are so prepared, then the body accepts the spirit and the spirit the body, and the bodies are made steadfast in the trial, and the *spirits* are held by the bodies so that they do not flee the fire.

Therefore *dissolve*, boil, *digest*, and *putrefy* the *Elements* in their dung <note>a common alchemical term for a gentle, moist heat source, often literally horse manure</note> until the end, and bury them after every boiling, so that the *separated* things may be all the better purified and become a living *Mercury* in the form of a clear water. However, if you do not divide the Stone—that is, the fifth substance <note>the "Quintessence" or the purest essence beyond the four elements</note>—through the four *Elements*, then know that

# Concerning the Philosophical Stone.

<margin>The importance of the beginning.</margin>
The foundation must be present; however, if the foundation was deficient, then the final completion will also be deficient. Therefore, see to it that the elements are purified of their impurities to the highest degree of perfection through ascending and descending <note>Refers to distillation and sublimation</note>; then, a perfect operation will follow from them.

Know furthermore that the office of the medicine of the first order is not only occupied with removing superfluities, but also with replacing deficiencies. For to <term>prepare</term> is to take away what is excessive and to replace what is lacking. For that which is heavy cannot be led into the heights except by the addition of the light; and the light or volatile can be brought to the bottom or <term>fixed</term> <note>To make a substance resistant to heat so it no longer evaporates</note> in no other way than by mixing it with the heavy. 

Likewise, the warm cannot be tempered or <term>prepared</term> in any way without the addition of the cold, nor the cold without the warm, nor the moist without the dry, nor the dry without the moist, nor the hard without the soft, nor the soft without the addition of the hard. But when they are properly wedded to one another in an alternating manner, then a tempered <term>substance</term> is born from them, which neither the power of fire can overcome, nor the impurity of the earth destroy, nor the sliminess of the water make turbid, nor the impurity of the air darken. # On the Philosopher's Stone.

It makes [the substance] constant, enters it, makes it compact, multiplies it, gathers it together, and brings it back to life; it purifies and enlightens all the dead, and causes them to rise again, after the cold and moisture have first been removed and the heat and dryness have been made manifest, in such a way that they no longer flee from the fire. Therefore, whoever does not know all of this should keep his hand away from the Work until he knows it beforehand; and when he truly understands it, he will have cause to congratulate himself, because then the Work will proceed according to his wishes.

But when they are thus prepared, you can through Art achieve the <term>conjunction</term> <note>original: "conjunction" — the alchemical marriage or union of opposites</note> of the man and the woman, so that they together beget the Son of the Fire, who is held in such great value by all philosophers; and in this union (if you truly understand me) lies our entire mastery.

THE great Hermes <note>Refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational alchemical texts are attributed.</note> says: Whoever wishes to create benefit in this Divine Science, it is necessary for him to well recognize the *Principia* <note>original: "Principia"; the fundamental principles or first beginnings</note> or beginnings of this Art. If it is applied, it acquires the *qualities* of gold; if it is added to silver, it takes on the *qualities* of silver; with copper, those of copper; and so on in other metallic *species* <note>original: "specien"; refers to the specific types or categories of metals</note>. Therefore, there can be no water that could *dissolve* <note>original: "dissolviren"</note> the metallic *species* with a natural restoration, except for that which remains with them in *matter* and *form*, and which the dissolved metals can in turn *congeal* <note>original: "congeliren"; to solidify or thicken</note>. Furthermore, no water belongs to the bodies in their *solutions* <note>original: "solutionibus"</note> or dissolutions which does not remain with them during the *coagulations* <note>original: "coagulirungen"</note>; but *Mercury*, being a seed, does exactly this. For this reason, no water *dissolves* the body except that which is of its own kind, and which can be *thickened* <note>original: "inspissiret"</note> or condensed again by the bodies. Nor are the bodies *nourished* <note>original: "nutriret"</note> or fed toward the *generation* of that same *form*, except through that very same water for the *preservation* <note>original: "conservation"</note> of those *species* which have been *destroyed* <note>original: "destruirt"</note> from our *transmuting* body through the artistic mastery of the Work. Furthermore, the perfect bodies are never opened, *exalted* <note>original: "exaltiret"; raised to a higher chemical or spiritual state</note> or placed into a higher degree, or *multiplied*, except through this water, which is of the same essence as they are.

# On the Philosophical Stone.

For this substance which nourishes and multiplies (and nothing else in the whole world) is transformed into that very same species. And just as this same water dissolves, nourishes, and multiplies the bodies, and hides them within its belly, so they in turn congeal it; and that which was previously hard becomes soft, and the soft becomes hard. Therefore, whoever knows the art and secret of preparing the aforementioned Divine Water <note>A poetic term for the alchemical solvent or "mercury of the philosophers."</note> attains the secret of truth and the Art, which consists of dissolving the species and extracting the natures from the natures which lie powerfully hidden within them.

## Mercury.

The dissolving Mercury <note>The "mercury of the philosophers," a specialized solvent, not common quicksilver.</note> is that through whose action the metals are dissolved with a natural resolution, and their spirits are brought from potentiality into actuality <note>original: "de potentia in actum ducuntur"</note>. # On the Philosopher's Stone

The dissolving Mercury <note>original: "dissolvirende Mercurius"; in alchemy, this refers to a specialized solvent or "philosophical" mercury, not common quicksilver</note>, when it is entirely alone, does nothing special or fruitful toward generation <note>the alchemical process of "birthing" the Stone</note>.

The dissolving Mercury arises from and participates in two elements, namely Earth and Water.

The dissolving Mercury is the element of Earth, into which a small grain of Gold must be sown.

The dissolving Mercury destroys the Gold and resolves it into quicksilver, and makes it volatile.

The dissolving Mercury resolves the Gold into a water of its own form—that is, a running quicksilver, just as it is itself.

The dissolving Mercury is transformed into Gold and Silver; therefore, it can ascend higher, be exalted, and be made equal to all the Mercuries of the metals.

The dissolving Mercury draws the souls of all others to itself, cooks them, and carries them upward with it.

It has been said previously through the teachings of the Philosophers that we must of necessity irritate or provoke Nature; if, therefore, the dissolving Mercury should be dry, the solution will be hoped for in vain.

The female seed of the Stone <note>the passive, receptive principle in the alchemical marriage</note> should be taken in such a form that is equal to and closely related to the metals, and comes nearest to the metals.

It is of the highest necessity to take the seed of the Philosophical Medicine <note>another name for the Philosopher's Stone or the elixir</note>, which represents or introduces the dissolving Mercury.

The dissolving Mercury is of all metals

# Of the Philosophical Stone.

## Concerning the Dissolvable Body and its Work.

As far as the body is concerned, let it suffice for this time to name it merely by the name of **Litharge** <note>original: "Bleyglätte"; lead monoxide, often used as a starting material in alchemy</note> or simply the **Body**. This body, however, is ordained to endure all kinds of misery, for it must pass through fire and water and be born again; otherwise, it cannot enter into eternal rest. Its color is brown, reddish, and not shiny; its work, however, requires that it be dissolved and exalted, that it die away, and rise into the heights.

## Concerning the Conjunction of the Two Aforementioned.

When one now possesses these two—namely, the Spirit and the Body—and puts them together according to the proper proportion, another **Mercury** <term>Mercurius: here referring to the "Philosophical Mercury," a refined substance rather than common quicksilver</term> is produced from them, and such is that Mercury of which it is written:

> In Mercury is everything the Wise seek,
> Spirit, soul, and tincture are drawn from it.
<note>original Latin: "Est in mercurio quicquid quærunt Sapientes, Spiritus, atq; anima & tinctura trahuntur ab ipso"</note>

->That is:<-

> The Wise receive all that they desire
> From Mercury;
> Body, Spirit, and Soul are led out from it,
> And the Tincture is prepared therefrom.

This Mercury is moist in its vapor, not oily but viscous, of a great acidity, moderately subtle, and flees the violence of the fire quite easily.

And for this reason, the Philosophers have called it three things, and these three are one, and in one there are three; for the body, the spirit, and the soul are one, and all are from one, and whoever goes astray regarding this single thing in the beginning, the same works in vain.

The **tincture** is called the **soul**, the whole **composite** is the **body**, but the **spirit** is called the **volatile nature**, before it is fixed and made stable.

And likewise, if a pot is covered so that the vapors cannot escape, it does not appear that the water should become nothing. # Concerning the highly useful superfluous part and its operation.

The highly useful superfluity is an oil or a sliminess of the body which floats above the *menstruum* <note>original: "menstruo"; a technical term for a solvent or dissolving liquid used in alchemy</note> after its dissolution. It is necessary that the body be transformed into an oil, for unless it is converted in this way, it remains dense and solid within itself, and that which we seek will not come from it; indeed, a corruption of all the principles of this Art would follow.

Since we recognize through this description what the highly useful superfluity is, we wish to examine its operation from the writings of the philosophers in order to understand it all the better.

Thus says *Rosarius* <note>referring to the "Rosarium Philosophorum" or "Rosary of the Philosophers," a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise</note>: Whoever wishes to enter into our Rose Garden and there see and take possession of both white and red roses without that lowly thing—namely, without the superfluous black moisture with which our enclosures are opened—that person is compared to a man who wishes to walk without feet. For without that same lowly thing, the precious thing is never completed. The philosophers have honored such a lowly thing and said that it is a stone and not a stone, and they have called it by all manner of names.

In the first book of Genesis, in the first chapter: The Spirit of God hovered over the waters (and the beginning of generation is from Him); and likewise: A mist rose up from the earth.

# In what manner the superfluity is removed and washed away.

The knowledge of the removal and purification of the superfluity—both the useful and the useless—is a great secret <note>original: "Heimligkeit"</note> and known to very few. So it also happens to us in the **Work of the Stone** <note>The "Work of the Stone" refers to the Alchemical Magnum Opus, the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note>; and for that reason, you must sweep our **well** <note>The "well" or "fountain" is a metaphor for the vessel or the mercurial solvent used in the process.</note> with great diligence, very often, until everything proceeds well and rightly.

Thus also speaks our **Ripley** <note>George Ripley (c. 1415–1490), a famous English alchemist.</note>: When the **Earth** shall be disturbed and stirred up, then shall the **mountains** be displaced into the **heart of the sea**. <note>original: "Wenn die Erden wird turbiret... so werden die Berge versezt werden in das Hertz des Meers." This imagery refers to the dissolution of solids into a liquid state.</note>

Regarding the number of removals and the cleansing of the superfluity, our **Dastin** <note>John Dastin (c. 1293–1386), an influential English alchemist.</note> says thus in his **Rosary**: **Imbibe** <note>term: Imbibition; the process of adding liquid to a dry substance until it is saturated.</note> or soak, and sift the things (that is, the **sulfurs**) with a **spherical** or round sieve, and wash away the **blackness** seven times; and make everything into a pure and clear water; and as often as you soak it, so often let it gradually become dry again.

**Barsanetes** in the **Turba** <note>Referring to the "Turba Philosophorum" or Assembly of the Philosophers, one of the oldest European alchemical texts.</note> testifies to the very same, saying: Water is put therein seven times, until it entirely drinks in the moisture, and attains a constant power to strive against the fire, and then it is called a **rust**. <note>The term "rust" here likely refers to a stable, oxidized metallic state or a specific color change in the work.</note>

Likewise, the Philosopher **Herizerrem** says in his **Monad**: Take it out, and rub it, until it be washed seven times from all stench, and watery moisture, and burning blackness: Afterwards cook it, until it dries out, and becomes a parched earth, and take care that the **secret** <note>original: "arcanum"; the hidden essence or transformative substance.</note> does not smoke away and fly off.

## A Discourse on our Secret.

Above all things, it is to be noted that, insofar as our
Secret does not have within itself that which improves it,
it is of no use at all. Therefore the Ancients have

### Another Interpretation of the Three Dimensions.

So that you may better understand the three dimensions, some other philosophers interpret them in this way: The <term>extremity</term> <note>The outer limits or polar opposites of a substance</note> of our Stone is, on one side, <term>Mercury</term> <note>The fluid, volatile principle in alchemy</note>; on the other side, however, is the <term>Elixir</term> <note>The perfected medicinal or transformative substance</note> brought to complete fulfillment. ## Another Description of the Medi-
### cine of the First Order.

In the preparation of our wonderful mixture or highest secret, we must follow Nature: For as *Geber* <note>Referring to Jabir ibn Hayyan, the famous 8th-century alchemist</note> says, she works or *acts* <note>original: "agiret"</note> for herself; therefore we must well know three things: namely, what Nature is; how many natures there are; and in what manner Nature *operates*.

However, according to the opinion of *Aristotle* in the second book of his *Consultations on Physics* <note>original: "Physicæ consultationis"</note>, Nature is described thus:
**Nature is a beginning and cause of 
motion and of rest in that in 
which it exists primarily and for itself, 
and not by *accident* or chance;**
and according to the author of the book *The Perfect Mastery* <note>original: "perfecti Magisterii"</note>:
There are four natures (or if you would rather say: *complexions* <note>The balance of bodily humors or qualities</note> of the first qualities), namely: **heat and dryness** as in fire; **heat and moisture** as in the air; **moisture and cold** as in water; **cold and dryness** as in the earth. But all these *complexions* are unequal, and none among them is that which we seek, for we seek the *equal* <note>original: "æquale"</note> or balanced, harmonious essence. Regarding this, *Joannitius* <note>Hunayn ibn Ishaq, a prominent scholar and physician</note> says that the equal mixture is a unique one, when the body, by means of its governance, is called "without defect."

For when none of these natures overpowers the others, the body is then called "temperate" or harmonious; for it contains as much of one as the other, according to the proper proportioning of qualities as required by the *essence* <note>original: "esse"</note> or constitution of the body.

   Likewise, you must also note that by the little word "unfailing," as much is meant as: healthy, remote, *calcined* <note>term: calcination; the process of reducing a metal to a fine powder through heat</note>, *separated*, *purified*, *disposed*, dry, and clean from all cause of *corruption* <note>meaning decay or chemical breakdown</note>. And according to the words of Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a famous 8th-century alchemist</note>: Tin is a very white lead, and in it is an equality of *fixity* or *compactness* of two composing things, namely Mercury <note>original: "Quecksilber"</note> and (metallic) Sulfur.

   However, such equality between the *living silver* <note>original: "argento vivo" or quicksilver</note> and sulfur is not to be understood according to the quantity in the first mixing, but rather in the quality. This is because the sulfur does not overpower the mercury in *acting* or working, nor does the mercury overpower the sulfur in its passive *quality*, since there is an equal *proportion* of measure between them in the white lead. So also says Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note>: O you sons of the wise, there are seven metals (or rather six, for mercury is not a metal, but the *matter* of metals), the first of which is their best, Gold.

King and Head: Since gold is indestructible, possesses no superfluity, and is the most perfect and complete among all combustible <note>The author uses "combustible" here to refer to metals that can be altered by fire, though gold is the exception that withstands it.</note> metals; and is a substance that rejoices in the fire and persists within it, which is neither corrupted by any cement <term>cement: a powder used in alchemy to purify gold through heat</term>, nor burned by any consuming thing, nor mortified or eaten away by the green coloring-water or aqua fortis <note>original: "Scheidwasser" — literally "parting water," referring to nitric acid used to separate gold from silver.</note>; because its temperament <note>original: "complexion" — the balance of the four qualities.</note> is tempered and most perfect, and of a balanced nature in heat, moisture, cold, and dryness. And what, therefore, is superfluous or lacking in gold? Certainly nothing; for should there be any deficiency or superfluity in its substance (which is utterly denied), just as such is found in lead and other combustible metals (in whose natural mixing a combustible superfluity has for the most part remained), then the greatest inconvenience or absurdity would follow. Namely, to speak plainly, that it could gradually be brought out of its state and reduced to nothing, which is ridiculous to say and in fact patently false. For gold should have nothing volatile or evaporable within it, just as it cannot have, whereas such things happen to the other destructible metals. Indeed, let such a foolish fantasy be far from the minds of those practicing philosophy, that gold could in any way be annihilated. And for this reason, the Sages have given it the preference and held it in high esteem, saying that gold is in such a state among the metals as the sun is among the stars; for she brings with her light and shine all—

(According to *Aristotle* in his *Categories* <note>Aristotle's "Categories" is a foundational text in logic and philosophy; here the author applies his types of motion to alchemy.</note>) there are six types of motion: namely, *corruption* or destruction, *generation* or birthing, *augmentation* or increasing, *diminution* or decreasing (which we call the process of becoming fixed), *alteration* or change, and the change of place. For this time, however, we shall let the others rest and take up only *corruption*—and even then, not in its entirety, for it encompasses many *species* <note>types or varieties</note> within itself. Instead, we shall go through only one of these (which is called *putrefactio* or rot), as it serves our purpose particularly well.

Thus Nature, which never rests, employs all kinds of motion for her *operation*; but especially the *corruption* of all things. Here, *corruption* and *putrefaction* have the same meaning. Of this, *Hermes* <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> says in his *allegory* thus:

> Know that the beginning of the Art is the
> Raven’s Head, which flies without wings
> in the blackness of the night and the
> clarity of the day; from whose bitterness,
> which is in its throat, the coloring is taken,
> and a pure water from its back.

Therefore, the Raven’s Head is nothing other than the blackness of the night; for just as such things are black and dark when compared to the day, so too is the *corrupted spirit* <note>original: "corrumpirte spiritus"</note> to be regarded in comparison to the pure spirit which arises out of the *corruption* and is *extracted* through our artistic mastery.

Note this concerning *corruption* or destruction: in the works of Nature, there is a *corruption* of things, but no scattering of the parts, unless they be superfluous parts and useless for *generation*...

# Another Explanation of the Forementioned Things.

In order that this treatise may be of use to us, and indeed be sufficient, so that everything mentioned before may be understood all the better and more clearly; it is proper to know that the mercury <note>original: "Quecksilber"; in alchemy, this often refers to 'Philosophical Mercury,' a foundational substance rather than common quicksilver</note> from which our Stone takes its origin is *composed* of two things: namely of the body and spirit, man and woman, the ripe and the unripe. This is what *Calid* <note>Khalid ibn Yazid, an early Umayyad prince and famed legendary alchemist</note> the *philosopher* and King in *Albania* openly teaches when he says: "You should know that in the beginning of our work we have no other business than with two things; and no more than two are seen, nor more than two touched; nor do more than two enter into the beginning, middle, or end of our mastery." And the very same is testified by *Hermes* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy</note> when he says: "Its father (namely of the first *composition*) is the Sun, but its mother is the Moon." In the same vein *Morienus* <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist</note> also speaks, saying: "The confidence consists in two: namely in the Moist, that it *dissolves* <note>original: "solvire"</note> the Dry, and in the Dry, that it *coagulates* <note>original: "coagulire"</note> the Moist." But in these two there are, according to their power, four *qualities*: for in the greater *seed* <note>original: "sperma"; used here in the biological sense of a generative starting material</note> as in the worthier part, the two worthier *elements* are contained in their *qualities*, namely Fire and Air;

Regarding this, Dastinus <note>John Dastin (c. 1293–1386), an influential English alchemist known for his correspondence with Pope John XXII.</note> says: **"That all the colors of the world will appear when the blackening moisture is dried up."** Yet you should not turn your attention to such colors, since they are not true colors; for it often turns red, and frequently yellow; it often dissolves and *coagulates* <note>original: "coagulirt"; the process of a liquid thickening into a solid</note> before the true whiteness. It also becomes green before the whiteness, and black-blue, and violet-colored; likewise, the color of the peacock <note>The "Peacock's Tail" (Cauda Pavonis) is a stage characterized by a rapid play of iridescent colors.</note> appears before the whiteness, which whiteness is always to be expected as the goal you desire to reach in the first work, and which afterwards transforms into no other true color except red. Note this well.

# On the Philosopher’s Stone.

Note that the cause of the diversity of colors comes from the alteration of our Mercury <term>Mercurius: the "quicksilver" or feminine, volatile principle of the work</term> through its own Sulfur <term>Sulphur: the masculine, combustible principle that provides form and color</term>.

One must also know this: although it is often said by the Philosophers <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers to historical alchemists like Geber or Hermes Trismegistus.</note> to put the material in its vessel and seal it very tightly, it is nevertheless enough that it be put in and sealed only once, until such time as you accomplish the entire Mastery <note>original: "Meisterschafft," referring to the completion of the Great Work</note> through Divine Will. Anything beyond that is of the evil one: for if you were to put something in multiple times, the Stone would be transformed into neither Whiteness nor Redness <note>The "White" (albedo) and "Red" (rubedo) are the final two major stages of the alchemical process.</note>; therefore, they have spoken in such a way only to hide the Art.

Indeed, it is certainly the same in the generation of a human being: the seed is never placed into the female womb more than once. For if it were to be put in again at another time, one would only spoil the other—either because of the completely unripened rawness <note>original: "crudität"</note>, or the entry of air, or the superfluity of material. For this reason, women who mix with many and various men very seldom conceive; or if they do conceive, they give birth to a premature birth. For if one puts together the raw and the cooked, the ripe and the unripe, it provides no nourishment for the work, but rather a corruption of the same; for the fruit is nourished solely by the menstrual blood <note>In medieval and early modern embryology, it was believed the fetus was formed from the union of seed and retained menstrual blood.</note> and lives until it comes forth into the light.

From which it then appears, that we do not [need] many things...
