# Of Nature and Art, and their
# Distinction.

Since it is said by many philosophers—and indeed with complete truth—that the art of Alchemy <note>original: "Archimiæ," a variant of Alchimia</note>, that is, the art of transmutation or the transformation of metals, is an art and work of Nature, and that in such work we must follow Nature: it is therefore fitting, before one undertakes this work and its practice or manual labor, to treat somewhat of its primary materials. Although such has already been recounted more than sufficiently in the preceding sections, it will nonetheless not be useless to add a little more at this point for a clearer understanding. I say, therefore, that certain mineral materials are created by Nature alone and not by Art; but after they have been created by Nature and are now in the power of the artist, Nature prepares them once again, either in that preparation which precedes the first philosophical operation <note>the initial cleansing of raw matter</note> or the first philosophical work, or else in the philosophical work itself, so that they are made fit for a generation <note>the "birth" of the stone</note>.

# Concerning the Philosopher's Stone

Therefore, *Clangor* <note>original: "Clangor Buccinae" (The Sound of the Trumpet), a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise</note> says: **Our Stone is found created by Nature, and requires nothing else than that the artist comes to the aid of Nature, and brings the same from imperfection to perfection.** Therefore, Nature first brings forth the matter and creates it, and afterwards it is assisted by Art.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;For that reason, the first and foremost cause of the birth of metals in the work of Nature is natural, but the second is artificial; yet this latter achieves nothing without the former: for it would be in vain to want to make an electuary <note>term: "Latwerge" - a medicinal paste or conserve made by mixing powders with honey or syrup</note> if the matter for it were not created by Nature. And it is therefore known that on both sides one is helped by the other, namely Nature by Art, and Art by Nature; and again, both of these are beneficial to the work of both Nature and Art. The difference between Nature and Art in the works of Nature consists in this: that Nature acts or works internally, but Art works externally. And if you only have the good knowledge to dispose and govern Nature externally, she will—in everything she requires until the final end of perfection—satisfy herself and you also internally.

# On the Generation of Metals within the Earth.

->Concerning the Philosophical Stone.<-

Rasis <note>Rhazes, or Abu Bakr al-Razi (c. 865–925), a Persian physician and alchemist highly influential in Western alchemy</note> says that everything created here below the circle of the moon by the highest Creator participates in or partakes of the four elements. This is not according to outward appearance, but according to their virtue <note>The inherent power or essential quality of a substance</note>. For we call the watery element the moisture of the water itself. We call the air the nature of the air itself. But the fire we call that power which it possesses, by which it burns, calcines <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or ash</term>, and melts. The earth is a thick and coarse body <note>original: "corpus"</note> in itself. And thus, only water and earth are seen and touched by us, while the other two are understood to be within these both.

It follows from this that all metals found in the earth are generated from the four elements, just like Mercury <note>original: "Mercurius"</note>, which is the mother, matter, and root of them all. When this Mercury is heated, the elements within it are moved through their own motion <note>original: "motum"</note>, and the natural heat is stirred by such movement. Namely, the fire and the air contained in the Mercury are moved at once and gradually brought into elevation, because such elements are worthier than the water and the earth of the Mercury. Nevertheless, moisture and coldness prevail in Mercury, for the heavenly movements stir the other movements of the natural heats <note>original: "calorum"</note>, and through such movements of the Mercury, the four elements of the Mercury—that is, its four qualities—are moved. Afterward, however, over a long period of time, dryness overcomes...

# On the Philosophical Stone

Since the Mercury of lead, as well as the Mercury of gold, is a pure, clear fire, the fire would not flee in such a case; for fire does not drive away its own kind, but rather rejoices in the fire as its equal. Thus, the other metals—gold excepted—flee from the fire because they are still cold and moist, though one more than another, according to how much they participate more or less in coldness and moisture. They flee from that which is contrary to them and cannot endure it, for every thing by nature flees its <note>original: "contrarium"</note> opposite or adversary, and conversely takes pleasure in its own kind.

From this it follows that gold is nothing other than a pure, clear fire in Mercury, since it does not retreat from the violent fire, whereas other metals cannot suffer the fire—though one more than another, according to how much they agree more or less with the fire's <term>complexion</term> <note>The "complexion" refers to the specific balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>. In such a manner, you can understand the <term>complexion</term> of the metals and their nature.

For Sulfur is nothing other than a pure, clear fire—that is, the Warm and Dry—which is hidden within Mercury. It digests or ripens the coldness and moisture in Mercury according to the <note>original: "varietät"</note> variety or multiplicity of the degrees of "cooking" and the <note>original: "alteration"</note> transformation into different metallic forms. # On the Transformation of Natures.

The transformation of natures is nothing other than a circular rotation of the elements; for they are, by their own aptitude, convertible one into another, and are therefore *generated*, *corrupted*, and *altered* among themselves. And certainly, our *operation* <note>The "Great Work" or process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> is a circular transformation of natures—that is, a wonderful and friendly binding together of the opposing elements (through the mediation of their middle-natures). Therefore, *Aristotle* says in the *sixth book of Physics*: <note>original: "sexto physicorum"</note> It is impossible for a transition to exist between *contraries* or opposing things from one to the other, unless it happens through their middle-nature.

Therefore, that which is Hot is not transformed into the Cold, except solely through the Moist, which is its medium; likewise, water is not transformed into fire, unless it is first converted into air; in the same way, the earth is not changed into air, unless it is first converted into water. For fire and water are opposing elements, or elements standing in *contrariety* to one another, or the furthest *extremities*; air and earth, however, are the medium between them. For just as water is below the air, so is the air above by the fire; therefore, water *opposes* fire, just as earth opposes air, because water and air agree with each other in moisture: fire and earth in dryness. The earth is transformed immediately into fire

Regarding this, another Philosopher speaks thus: **He who knows how to transform the Dry into the Cold, and the Cold into the Moist, and the Moist into the Warm, and the Warm into the Dry, he shall attain the entire Mastery.** <note>The "Mastery" refers to the successful completion of the Great Work or the creation of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>

Therefore, join these natures together—namely the male and the female, the warm, cold, moist, and dry—in actual practice, and nourish them with **living water** <note>original: "lebendigem Wasser"; likely referring to mercurial water or a potent solvent used in alchemy</note>, so that the natures may be altered and transformed into other natures, and that the natures may appear through the natures. For Nature has ordered it quite well, that the elements should communicate their qualities to one another in a reciprocal manner, insofar as circular transformations arise from them, and from the circular transformation comes the transformation of the elements. For the earth communicates its dryness to the fire, the fire its warmth to the air, the air its moisture to the water, the water its coldness to the earth, and the earth again its dryness to the fire. And thus the matter of the earth desires, in a circular fashion, to be under the form of fire; for the "thirsty" fire acts naturally upon the earth and transforms the matter of the earth into its own form.

There are, however, four principal ways of transforming the natures into one another: namely **dissolving, washing, re-infusing, and congealing.** <note>original: "solviren, abwaschen, wieder aufgiessen, und congeliren." These represent the chemical stages of the alchemical process.</note>

# On the Philosopher’s Stone.

The first path or method <note>original: "modus"</note> occurs through dissolving <note>original: "solviren"</note>; that is, the body must first be dissolved. The second is through cleansing or washing away <note>original: "abluiren"</note>, for it must be washed clean. The third is through pouring back out <note>original: "reduciren"</note>, for the moisture must be put back onto the dry substance or restored. The fourth is through congealing <note>original: "congeliren"</note> with a gentle fire; and in these four types consists the true transformation of natures.

Furthermore, dissolving is the same as dividing or separating from one another, breaking down <note>original: "corrumpiren"</note>, and creating the first matter <note>original: "primam materiam"</note> or the initial material or nature.

Cleansing or washing away is also the same as burying in the earth <note>original: "inhumiren"</note>, distilling, ascending and descending, calcining <note>technical term: heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile substances</note>, correcting the natures, and softening the coarse parts, so that one nature may enter into the other in a harmonious way, and they may become one together from the substance of a single nature.

Restoring or pouring back out is the same as waxing <note>original: "inceriren"; making a substance soft like wax</note> or making volatile, fattening <note>original: "impinguiren"</note> or impregnating, refining, and uniting the elements, so that one can act or work upon the other: namely, the fire into the earth, the earth into the water, the water into the air, the air into the fire; for they are fluid, and in a spiritual manner of a single flow, and of "inceration" or liquefaction.

Congealing is marrying together, resolving, and holding the opposing natures; for they are united with one another, and one is easily held by the other, which is impossible without the dissolution and the washing of the natures.

From this it follows that dissolution is the beginning of the whole work; likewise, the washing is a pacifying of the natures; for that which is washed away,

Thus, the first *method* <note>original: "modus"</note> is *sublimation*. ## Of the Vessel, its Form
->and material.<-

# On the Philosophical Stone.

In this second governance of the fire, the *Sulfur* <note>original: "Sulphur"; in alchemy, the active, combustible principle</note> dries out the *Mercury* <note>original: "Mercurium"; the fluid, metallic principle</note>; this heat must not be strong, but moderate. This whiteness is a color of regeneration <note>the stage known as the Albedo or "whitening"</note> and represents the halfway point of the dry desiccation. And because the white is a half-boiled essence, it requires no great heat; this whiteness lasts through two distillations and 24 days.

Note herewith that when the matter <note>original: "materi"</note> has been brought to whiteness, it can then no longer be corrupted or destroyed.

The sign of the first perfection—namely of the entire matter—is the appearance of a small, hair-like, yellowish circle which appears around the matter and on the sides of the vessel.

Such heat must now be strong and is compared to the heat of the sun when it is in the sign of the <term>Leo</term><note>The Lion; the zodiac sign associated with the peak of summer and the greatest strength of the sun.</note>: for this is the house of its dignity. And because the Red is a perfectly ripened essence, it requires a strong fire so that everything together may be transformed into fire, so that it no longer fears any fire; for then our <term>Dragon</term><note>A common alchemical symbol for the volatile matter being "tamed" or fixed by heat.</note> shines with solar <term>Fixity</term><note>The state where a substance is stable in fire and will not evaporate.</note> and is adorned through such brilliance with heavenly and earthly powers.

In this regard, let it be remembered that among these degrees of heat, each one must double the previous one.

Note also that many names are given to it according to the various colors that appear during the "governments" or stages of the process. ## The Regime of Autumn.

The fourth time, however, is of a cold and dry complexion <note>In humoral theory, "complexion" refers to the specific combination of qualities—heat, cold, moisture, dryness—governing a body or season</note>, and is called the Autumn, in which the fruits are gathered.

# Concerning the Philosophical Stone

Consider also what the great *Rosarius* <note>likely referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum* or "Rose Garden of the Philosophers," a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise</note> puts forward with the same opinion in these words:

> Take care that you do not start your solution <note>original: "solution"; the process of dissolving a solid substance into liquid form</note> (which belongs to the Winter) too hastily, intending to perform it before the proper time: For such haste is a sign that no true conjunction <note>original: "conjunction"; the chemical and spiritual union of opposites, such as male and female or sulfur and mercury</note> will be able to follow. Therefore, let your external fire be moderately warm, in such a way that it does not exceed the internal heat; namely, so that the internal heat retains its moisture, which it naturally carries with it. For if the external heat is excessively strong, then the fatty moisture, which is mixed with a subtle earth, flees away from the overly violent fire and does not remain in the body.

In the same way, Count Trevisan <note>Bernard of Treviso, a 15th-century alchemist known for his search for the Stone</note> also speaks of the fire in this manner:

> Know that a cold fire (that is, an overly gentle fire) neither alters nor mixes things together (and is therefore neither useful nor harmful), just as the violent fire prevents the movement of them both (that is, the mixing with one another).

So also says Isaac <note>likely referring to Isaac Hollandus, a Dutch alchemist</note>:

> A great fire ruins the work, but an overly gentle one never does.

Likewise, Mary <note>Mary the Prophetess, an ancient alchemical figure credited with inventing the *balneum Mariae* or water bath</note> speaks of this:

> The violent fire prevents the conjunction and tints the White into a useless redness.

## The Medicine of the Second Order.

The Medicine of the Second Order is that <term>preparation</term> <note>original: "præparation"</note> of the Stone which follows immediately upon the first; and it is called our perfect preparation: it is also called the <term>fixing</term> <note>original: "figirung"; the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat</note>, the <term>fermentation</term>, the completion of the Stone, and the perfect <term>conjunction</term> of the elements; it is also called by <term>Geber</term> <note>An 8th-century Arabic alchemist, Jabir ibn Hayyan, whose Latinized works were foundational to European alchemy</note> the "Short Work."

# On the Philosopher’s Stone.

The ferment of the Stone for the White work is Silver, and for the Red work it is Gold. Without ferment and fermentation, neither Gold nor Silver can be obtained, nor anything else that shares their nature. Therefore, so that Silver or Gold may be generated, you must join the ferment with its own white or red sulfur, so that it can generate its like in both nature and color; for every like generates its like. For the ferment—namely Gold—tinctures and transforms its sulfur into a lasting and penetrating medicine. Therefore, Empedocles the Philosopher says:

> **He who knows how to tincture the ferment with the sulfur arrives at the highest secret, which is called White Sulfur.**

To tincture is as much as to change a tinctured or colored thing into its own nature through the process of staining, and to remain with it without any separation, so that the fixing agent, the coloring agent, and that which is colored possess one single nature.

The white sulfur is a <term>body</term> <note>original: "corpus"</note> composed of the pure essence of the metals, which is otherwise called Mercury. This has been brought from its potentiality into actuality <note>original Latin: "deductum de eorum potentia in actum"</note> through the mastery of all the principles of the medicine of the first order. You should also note that the perfectly finished <term>Elixir</term> <note>The ultimate medicinal or transformative substance in alchemy</note> of the philosophers is a bodily tincture which has been extracted from the perfect metallic bodies by the help of true <term>solution</term> <note>original: "solucion"; the dissolving of a solid into liquid</note> and perfect, natural <term>congealing</term> <note>original: "congelation"; the thickening or solidifying of a substance</note>.

# On the Philosopher's Stone.

Or rather: It is a body <term>corpus; the physical substance of the alchemical work</term> that is composed of the very purest and clearest species, and is an antidote and medicine for all bodies that require curing and purging, whether they be animal or mineral.

The perfect Elixir of the Philosophers is composed of three parts: namely, of the **lunar stone**, of the **solar stone**, and of the **mercurial stone**. <note>In alchemy, lunar refers to Silver, solar to Gold, and mercurial to Quicksilver or the "Mercury of the Sages."</note>

In the lunar stone consists the white sulfur; in the solar, the red sulfur; and the mercurial stone encompasses both natures, namely the white and the red, and is the foundation of the entire art of transformation <term>transmutation</term> and the strength of the entire mastery. Therefore, Rhazes <note>original: "Rafis"; refers to the 9th-century Persian physician and alchemist Abu Bakr al-Razi</note> says: The white and the red come and spring from one root, that is, from Mercury, without the addition of any other thing that would be of a different genus. And Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the "Father of Chemistry"</note> says that the lunar and solar stones are of one and the same essence, for they are both made from the unique Mercury. And Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, the influential Persian polymath</note> says: Whoever knows how to bring forth our medicine—that is, our highly excellent, finished Elixir—from the unique Mercury, he is a researcher of the most magnificent work.

*Hermes* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> says: When the smoke becomes pure and white, it will be ready to be *joined* <note>original: "conjungiren"</note> with its soul—that is, with the purity of the two lights—and with the body—that is, with the oil of the glass—but not otherwise.

But above all things, I admonish you that you frequently take this general rule to heart in your mind, and consider for what reasons I have included it.

### A general Rule.

Every nature naturally desires to be brought to perfection, and conversely, it dreads and flees destruction; and for that reason, it eagerly accepts that which improves it.

However, I do not consider it unserviceable to remind you briefly once more how far the Medicine of the first order extends, namely:

The final limit of the Medicine of the first order—that is, of the <term>transmutation</term><note>The transformation of one substance into another.</note> of the cooked and the raw, toward which the artist is naturally directed—is the substance of the white <term>Sulphur</term><note>In this context, "Sulphur" refers to a philosophical principle of stability and fire, not just the common chemical element.</note> that does not burn; which, when it shall be transformed, is the first and most immediate material of our <term>Elixir</term><note>The "Elixir" or "Stone" is the goal of the work, capable of perfecting metals and curing disease.</note>, the first and most immediate nature, which is nevertheless altered or changed by the warmth of its body—namely, with that alteration through which it can more characteristically and closely take on its form.

Likewise, in the book called *Flores Sapientum* or **The Flowers of the Wise**, it is said: The Medicine of the first order, which nature makes (for it is a work of nature), is purely and solely the cause of simple perfection.

## What is Fermentation?

Fermentation is an *incorporation* or embodiment of the soulful essence; a *restoration* or re-establishment of the taste; an *inspiration* or quickening of the scent; and a perfection of the essences. The reason for its invention, however, was this: namely, so that the tinting agent and that which is tinted might be brought from potentiality into actuality <note>original: "de potentia in actum" — a Scholastic philosophical term meaning moving from a state of possibility to a state of realized action</note>.

Know, however, that in each and every *fermentation* one must take the highest care that the vessels do not perhaps break; this you must know, for it is a great *secret* <note>likely referring to the buildup of pressure during the chemical reaction</note>.

## Of the Ferments.

The ferments are of many kinds, namely simple and mixed.

The simple ferments are those which have no admixture at all, just as the elements are when one understands them quite simply for themselves, such as the souls which are *extracted* from their bodies.

The *mixed ferments* <note>original: "fermenta composita"</note> are when certain things are mixed with others, such as the bodies which are brought into the nature of sulfur and *conjugated* with their *oils*.

There are also sulphuric ferments of the imperfect bodies, which are called middle-ferments; but know for certain, that if you [do not have] the per-

# On the Philosopher’s Stone.

If you cannot bring the perfect bodies back into <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurium"; the liquid metallic principle of alchemy</note>, then you can bring neither a simple nor a composite <term>ferment</term> <note>an agent used to "leaven" or transform base matter into gold</note> into its <term>prime matter</term> <note>original: "primam materiam"; the original, undifferentiated substance from which all things are made</note> or initial essence; and if you do not have the aforementioned ferments, you cannot lead the Stone to its final completion.

Know, however, that there are two kinds of <term>prime matter</term> or initial essence: namely, a near one and a distant one. The near <term>prime matter</term> is quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, but the distant one is water; for the quicksilver was previously water, and afterwards became quicksilver. But the bringing back of the perfect bodies into <term>Mercury</term> and into their first matter is, in a particular way, nothing other than a <term>resolution</term> <note>original: "resolution"; a breaking down or dissolving</note> or re-dissolving of the perfect, fixed, white, and red congealed matter, through which <term>resolution</term> that which was locked is opened by the entry of one nature into the other. Furthermore, you must also note that the <term>ferments</term> must be prepared in the best possible way before one undertakes the <term>fermentation</term>.

The <term>preparation</term> of the <term>ferments</term> before the <term>fermentation</term> consists in this: that they must pass through the transforming principal-governances <note>original: "regimina principalia convertentia"; the primary stages of the alchemical process</note> of our mastery; since it is necessary for you that, first, a calcined powder be made through <term>liquefaction</term> <note>melting or making liquid</note>; second, a dissolved powder through <term>dissolution</term>; third, a well-<term>indurated</term> <note>hardened</note> or toughened powder through <term>congelation</term> <note>thickening or freezing</note>; fourth, a sublimated powder through <term>separation</term> or parting.

## Concerning our **dissolution**, and how it comes to pass.

Our **dissolution** is a re-melting of our dry and fixed **matter** into water; the reason for its invention is so that its internal nature may be turned outward, and that it may be rendered suitable for **distillation**.

The method for performing our **dissolution** is as follows: After our Stone has been prepared in the fire and cleansed of all dross—that is, impurity—namely (which you must note) after the whitening and the philosophical spiritual washing, which was explained clearly enough to you in the preceding sections; then, rub it upon a stone into a very **fine** <note>original: "subtilen"</note> powder and **fix** it strongly. Afterward, **dissolve** it in our sky-colored vinegar <note>A common alchemical term for a specific acidic solvent, often distilled vinegar or a mineral acid</note>; thus it will certainly **dissolve** (in its certain and **determined** time) into a very clear water, much like spring water. ## What our Multiplication is.

Our Multiplication <note>In alchemy, multiplication refers to the process of increasing the quantity or the potency of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> is nothing other than an increasing and multiplying of the natural heat / which is the sulfur that does not burn within the matter of the mercury; For it is certain / that mercury is, in its substance, the matter of the metals / wherein its clarity has been embodied; for the metals require nothing but a substantial nature / and the substance into which the tincture <note>A "tincture" is the spiritual or medicinal essence capable of transforming base metals into gold or silver.</note> of the sulfur is infused or embodied / must be of such a material / which is free from all combustion, and also pleasing and agreeable to all metals / and that the aforementioned substance be of such a quality / that it can be fixed <note>To "fix" a substance means to make a volatile spirit solid and resistant to fire.</note> without the consumption of its own moisture / and without the burning of its own substance: and therefore it is necessary / that the tincture of the sulfur follows such a substance / and be bound therein / if you wish it to be a tincture of the metals: and all of this is mercury; Therefore it is said / that such mercury, along with ignition or fieriness, is a cause of the multiplication and perfection of all metals / and the metals are that / from whose spirit every white and red Stone <note>The "white stone" transmutes metals into silver, while the "red stone" transmutes them into gold.</note> is composed / and the spirit of the metals is that / wherein the natures of the metals rest / and this spirit is called mercury through the consideration of the Alchemists <note>original: "Archimisten"</note> / and such mercury is, in its substance, the matter of the metals / as was said before.

# On the Philosopher's Stone.

## A General Rule.

Unless the perfect bodies <note>The "perfect bodies" refer to gold and silver, which alchemists believed were the final, completed stage of metallic evolution.</note> are brought back into a running mercury <term>mercurium: a liquid, flowing state of matter</term> and a dry water, they cannot be multiplied; for nothing further comes from a thing that is already perfect, since it has already been completed by nature and our craftsmanship.

For example: A fermented and baked bread is perfect in its state or essence, and has come to its final end; you cannot ferment anything further with it. The same applies to silver in the "white work" <note>The *albedo* or white stage of the alchemical process, resulting in silver</note> and to gold in the "red work" <note>The *rubedo* or red stage, the final goal resulting in gold</note>. Pure silver or gold has been brought into a solid and fixed body <note>original: "corpus"</note> through the trial of fire, and is considered by the philosophers to be impossible to use for further fermentation; unless one has the first matter <term>materi: the primordial substance from which all metals grow</term> of the metals, in which the silver or gold may be dissolved back into its initial essence and into its commingled elements. 

Therefore, let us take the matter from which gold and silver are made, and which—through the mediation of our craftsmanship—is promoted into the true ferment of the philosophers; and let us, with deep understanding, change such into a perfect matter, or into the form of the perfect bodies, and only then may we begin a new operation. For this reason, many who have worked philosophically in this matter have been deceived, because they abandoned the work just where it should have been started again. Hence Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational alchemical texts are attributed</note> says: "Oh, you dear sons of the doctrine, who [await] hoped-for..."

# On the Philosopher's Stone

This medicine, when prepared in its highest degree, is fire-resistant, penetrating, and coloring <note>original: "tingirend"; refers to the alchemical power to change the color and nature of a metal</note>. It reaches into the depths, making substances compact and enduring; it is exceedingly quick-flowing and transmutes all imperfect bodies, as well as mercury, into the finest silver. For as Rasis, Morienus, and Assiduus <note>Historical alchemical authorities: Rhazes (Persian physician), Morienus (legendary hermit), and likely a reference to an Arabic source</note> say: the earth becomes fixed as often as it is made white, because of the stability of silver, and it therefore colors things into silver. 

But afterward comes the "Leap of the Moon"—that is, the sublimation of the lunar moisture <note>original: "Lunarischen humidität"; refers to the volatile silver-principle</note>—and the "Circle of the Sun." For after the extraction of the solar spirit from its body, the earth becomes fixed with the stability of gold, and then colors things into gold. Just as Plato says: just as there is a white sulfur in every piece of silver, so there is a red sulfur in every piece of gold. And such a sulfur is not found on earth, as Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, the famous Persian polymath</note> says, except in these two bodies. 

And for this reason, we dissolve <note>original: "solviren"</note> these two bodies and prepare them subtly, so that from this same material we may obtain the sulfur and the mercury above the earth, from which gold and silver are generated within the earth. For such bodies are luminous, containing coloring rays which tint the remaining bodies into true whiteness and redness, without the mixture of any foreign thing. Therefore, silver is a tincture of whiteness, and gold is a tincture of redness; for with such bodies—namely silver and gold—mercury <note>original: "Mercurius"</note> mixes itself and is shaped by them. This is understood with deep intellect; however, such a thing is never achieved by any craftsman who possesses a coarse spirit or a dull understanding.

# On the Red Tincture and its Multiplication.

In order for the red tincture <note>The "Red Tincture" or "Red Lion" refers to the final stage of the Great Work, capable of transmuting metals into gold.</note> to be brought forth, the Mercury <note>original: "Mercurius"; here referring to the philosophical mercury or the "spirit" of the matter.</note> must be animated solely with the ferment of Gold, just as the white tincture is animated solely with the ferment of Silver.

To perform such a red work, however, it is said that it must happen in every way and with the same governance <note>The "governance" or "regimen" refers to the controlled management of the furnace heat.</note> as you have done in the White; so that it does not need to be started again from the beginning, but only multiplied. And for the solution <term>solution: the process of dissolving a solid body into liquid form</term> and the drying of the body, let as much of the raw Mercury be taken, and no more, than you took for the White; yet the heat should be increased at its proper time. 

But if you do not first make it white, you cannot make the true Red; and it is therefore absolutely necessary that it be white first, before it becomes red. For just as it is impossible to reach the third step from the first unless one first arrives at the second: so also you cannot proceed from the Black to the Yellow or the Red, unless you first travel through the White. For the yellowness is essentially composed of much White and little Red. Therefore, make the Black white, and the White red, and you shall attain the mastery.

Thus, it is to be diligently noted from this that when the pure, fine quicksilver <note>original: "Quecksilber"</note> is coagulated through the power of the white sulfur <note>original: "Schwefel"</note> which does not burn, this will be the best thing that the Alchemists can take in order to make their gold from it; and it will

# On the Philosophical Stone

It is therefore concluded that without the white sulfur, which does not burn, the Gold of the Philosophers <note>The "Gold of the Philosophers" refers to the perfected Alchemical Stone, not common bullion.</note> cannot be made; for the best sulfur of clear redness cannot become red unless it is first white. Therefore, the Philosophers first described the composition of the white sulfur for Silver, and afterward the red sulfur for Gold, because no gold can be created unless it was first silver. 

The white sulfur, however, is obtained from the purest substance of Mercury <note>original: "Quecksilber"</note>; for this alone contains within itself everything that we require. For this reason, an artist must be of a steadfast will in the Work, and not use many different things, but rather be intent only upon perfection; for our Art is not accomplished with a multitude of things. 

Therefore, when the Whiteness appears in the vessel and shines forth completely in all things, one is certain that the Redness is hidden within such Whiteness; and one must not then extract such Whiteness, but continue boiling <note>The term "boiling" or "decoction" refers to the prolonged application of steady heat in a sealed vessel.</note> until everything together becomes red. And certainly, the color of Redness is obtained solely from the completed boiling. And you shall accordingly reach the Redness after the Whiteness solely through boiling, with the continuation of the dry fire. 

For just as the Moon, after it is full, begins to decrease from day to day until finally nothing more of it is seen: so also the Whiteness and brightness of our white body begins to decrease through the boiling, until the entire Whiteness has passed away, and the Redness appears through the Yellowness; which shall also appear entirely and completely, provided that nothing of the watery moisture—which caused the Whiteness—has remained behind.

# A Brief Recapitulation of the Three Medicines.

First, we compose; that which is composed, we putrefy or rot; that which is rotted, we dissolve; that which is dissolved, we divide from one another; that which is divided, we purify; that which is purified, we unite; that which is united, we separate or part; that which is separated and distilled, we purify or cleanse; that which is made clean, we fix <note>term: fix (figiren) — to make a volatile substance stable and resistant to fire</note>; and thus is completed the Medicine of the first, second, and third order.

## Concerning the Virtues of this Wonderful Science or Philosophical Tincture.

Plato says: Whoever possesses this gift of God, possesses the highest mystery of Nature, the most precious secret <note>original: "Secret"</note> which surpasses all value, and is an incomparable and most dear treasure. Likewise says Herizartem the Philosopher <note>original: "Philoſophus"</note>: Whoever possesses this science has an incomparable treasure and is born under a most blessed constellation, being rich in this world with infinite riches above the kings and princes of this world. So also speaks Hermes: Whoever shall have performed this art but once, even if he should live a thousand times a thousand years thereafter and feed four thousand people every day, he would yet suffer no want. Senior confirms this with these words: He who possesses this science, from which the Elixir <note>term: Elixir — the perfected substance capable of transmuting base metals or healing the body</note> comes, is as rich as one who has fire, and can give of such fire to whomsoever

# On the Philosopher's Stone

The blood shall not rot, nor shall the phlegm <note>one of the four bodily fluids or 'humors' believed to control health</note> take the upper hand, nor the choler <note>yellow bile</note> become inflamed, nor the melancholy or black bile become too powerful. Indeed, it purifies the blood beyond all measure, purges the head of flowing humors, creates a good memory, prevents drunkenness, strengthens the stomach in its natural warmth, drives poison from the heart, moistens the arteries, disperses what has settled in the lungs, heals what is ulcerated or swollen, increases the radical moisture <note>the vital fluid or 'oil' thought to sustain life's flame</note>, promotes urine, breaks the stone <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>, stimulates and increases the seed, cleanses the waste from the breath-passages and keeps them pure, powerfully refreshes all members of the body and protects them from injury; and to speak *generally* <note>original: "generaliter"</note> of it, it heals all diseases—whether hot or cold, dry or moist—most certainly above all other medicines of the physicians, because it is of a hidden and subtle nature. And if the sickness is of one month's duration, it heals it in one day; if it is of a year, in twelve days; but if it is old and from a long time ago, in one month. In short: it drives out all evil humors and introduces good ones; it brings about love and honor to those who carry it with them, as well as safety and boldness, and victory in strife.

> And this is the experienced medicine of the philosophers, which our Lord **JESUS Christ**—who lives and reigns with the Father and Holy Spirit, true **GOD** for all eternity, Amen—wishes to grant to every true-hearted and pious seeker.

And herewith shall be concluded the explanation of the three *medicines* <note>original: "Medicinen"</note> of *Geber* <note>referring to Jabir ibn Hayyan, the legendary Arab alchemist</note>, which until now have never been presented so clearly.

# Translator’s Preface.

The content and the meaning of the following treatise is directed toward this: that its author gives us to understand how his preparation and purification of <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurii"; the liquid metal quicksilver, central to alchemical transformation</note> is performed in such a manner that he first produces for it an entirely pure <term>regulus of antimony</term> <note>the metallic heart or "little king" extracted from the ore</note> and <term>Mars</term> <note>alchemical name for Iron</note>. For this, he takes two parts of a good, long-striated <term>antimony</term> <note>original: "Spießglaſes"; stibnite ore, often found in needle-like crystal structures</note> (such as is brought from Hungary, Transylvania, and other gold-rich places) and one part of pure iron or steel. These he lets flow together in a blast furnace, and once they have flowed well—while they are in full flux—he pours a small spoonful of pure <term>saltpeter</term> <note>potassium nitrate, used as a flux to help separate metals</note> on top. This helps the pure mercurial part of the <term>antimony</term> to separate itself well from the sulfurous part and, being the heaviest, to settle at the bottom. The sulfurous part, however, being lighter, rises to the top; this is what one usually calls foam and slag. Then he pours it out into a <term>casting cone</term> <note>original: "Gießpuckel"; a conical iron mold used to separate the heavy metal "regulus" from the lighter slag</note> which has been slightly warmed and greased with wax or tallow, so that it does not stick firmly to the <term>casting cone</term> because of the grease. Thus, there settles in the <term>casting cone</term> the

# Preface

The <term>mercurial part</term><note>The volatile, metallic essence in alchemy, often associated with fluidity and shine.</note> settles into a pointed <term>king</term><note>original: "König"; a lump of purified metal that settles at the bottom of a crucible during smelting.</note>, while the <term>sulphurous part</term><note>The combustible or "oily" principle, often associated with impurities or "dross" in this context.</note> or the dross remains on top. When the mass has stood in the <term>casting cone</term><note>original: "Gießpuckel"; a conical mold used to separate pure metal from slag.</note> and become hard, he should turn it out and strike off the mercurial king. Let this melt once more in the <term>crucible</term>, and while in flux, add some <term>saltpeter</term><note>Potassium nitrate, used here as a flux to help separate impurities.</note> to it again. Then pour it back into the casting cone and let the mass harden. He will find that even more sulphurous <term>dross</term><note>original: "feces"; the waste or impure remains of a chemical process.</note> has separated from it, and the mercurial king has become even purer. Therefore, he should repeat this work several more times until, perhaps by the fifth such smelting, he finds the king at its purest and shining like silver. At that point, as a sign of its purity, it will represent a figure like a **star** on its surface.

From such a purified king—which in his opinion is the <term>Philosophical arsenic</term> or <term>chaos</term><note>The "prime matter" or fundamental starting material for the Great Work.</note>—he should take one part and two parts of fine **silver**. Melt these together and pour them out into a cake. Rub this into a powder and add three or four parts of <term>Mercury</term><note>original: "Mercurii"; quicksilver.</note>. Set them together overnight on warm sand, then rub them together until they accept one another and become an <term>amalgam</term>. He should <term>digest</term><note>To subject a substance to steady, gentle heat over time.</note> and wash this with water, perhaps using some <term>salt of urine</term><note>Ammonium chloride or similar salts derived from processed urine, used as a cleaning agent.</note> to assist in the washing, until the amalgam no longer gives off any blackness.

# EXPERIMENTS
## Or Practical Trials on the Preparation of the Philosophical Mercury:

### The Secret of the Philosophical Arsenic.

I took one part of the fiery dragon <note>original: "feuriger Drache"; likely referring to iron or a specific stibnite ore</note> and two parts of the magnetic body <note>original: "magnetischer Cörper"; often referring to the "magnesia" of the philosophers or a specific metallic ore</note>; these I prepared through a violent fire, whereby in the fifth preparation I obtained approximately eight ounces of the true arsenic <note>In alchemy, "arsenic" often refers to a crystalline salt or a specific stage of matter rather than the modern element alone</note>.

### The Secret of Preparing the Mercury with its Arsenic, so that it may cast off its dross.

I took one part of the best arsenic and made a marriage <note>A chemical union or alloy</note> with two parts of the Virgin Diana <note>original: "Jungfrauen Dianæ"; a symbolic name for silver</note>, bringing them both into one body. This I ground into a fine powder and prepared my Mercury with it, handling everything together in the heat until they were perfectly incorporated with one another. Subsequently, I purified them through the salt of urine <note>A source of ammonia used for cleaning metals</note> so that the dross <note>original: "feces"; the waste or impurities</note> might fall away, which I collected separately.

The prepared Mercury, because it was nonetheless still afflicted with some external impurity

# Three Tests for the Quality of Prepared Mercury

Take your Mercury, which has been prepared with its arsenic <note>In this context, "arsenic" likely refers to a specific crystalline salt or "philosophical" additive rather than common poison</note> from 7, 8, 9, or ten Eagles <term>Eagles: an alchemical term for the number of times a substance has been sublimated or distilled</term>; put it into a vial and seal it with the "lute of wisdom" <term>luto sapientiæ: a specialized airtight sealing clay used by chemists</term>. Place it in a sand-bath and let it stand in such heat as is necessary for sublimation, so that it rises and falls within the glass until it coagulates to a consistency a little thicker than butter. Continue this until complete coagulation and the whiteness of silver are achieved.

## Another Test

If the Mercury, when mixed with salt of urine <note>Ammonium chloride or related salts derived from processed urine</note>, transforms itself (by swirling the glass) into a white, delicate powder in such a way that the Mercury can no longer be seen, and in dryness and heat it returns of its own accord into a thin Mercury, then it is correct. However, it is even better if it breaks down into imperceptible droplets in the same way using spring water; for if even a single grain of the body <note>original: "gran corporis" — referring to metallic impurities or unrefined matter</note> remains within it, it will not allow itself to be divided into such tiny parts.

## Another Test

Distill it in a glass helm <note>The top part of a still, also called an alembic</note> from a glass flask; if it passes over and leaves nothing behind, then it is a good mineral-water.

# On the Preparation of Mercury

## The Manual Processing
## of this Mixture

You must grind this aforementioned mixture to the finest consistency upon a marble slab, and thereafter wash it with vinegar and sal ammoniac <note>ammonium chloride, used as a flux and cleaning agent in alchemy</note> until all black dross <note>original: "feces"</note> departs from it. Afterward, sweeten <note>wash away</note> all saltiness and sharpness with spring water, and subsequently dry it on a clean paper, turning it to and fro with the tip of a knife until all remaining moisture has evaporated.

## The Placement of the Fruit into the
## Philosophical Egg

Now you must place the said well-dried mixture into an egg-shaped glass, which should be very clear and transparent, and the size of a chicken egg. No more than 4 lots <note>a historical unit of weight, approximately 60 grams or 2 ounces</note> of material should be put into such a glass, and the glass must be hermetically sealed <note>melted shut to be airtight</note>.

## The Governance of the Fire

Furthermore, you must have a furnace ready in which a perpetual fire can be maintained, and know how to apply the first degree of sand-heat <note>a sand bath, used to provide even, gentle heat</note> therein. In this warmth, the dew of our mixture rises and circulates itself, and this continues on and on, day and night, without any intermission, etc. In such a fire, the spirit will die, and the body will be renovated or renewed, and finally, the soul will be glorified or magnified, and newly reunited with the immortal and indestructible body; and thus, a new heaven is made.

## Preface concerning this Dialogue.

**I**t is not difficult to guess why the author has called himself *Agricola*—that is, the Peasant or Farmer—namely, because his given name was Georgius <note>The name George derives from the Greek 'Georgos', meaning earth-worker or farmer.</note>, which signifies the very same thing. However, why he added the word *Rhomæus* or "the Roman" to it remains beyond conjecture, unless perhaps he was a follower of the Roman Catholic religion; it cannot be guessed with certainty. Furthermore, this is of no particular concern to the reader, whose sole purpose is to lay a firm foundation from good books. To this end, these small treatises can be of no small assistance, as their author was highly experienced in the <term>Hermetic Philosophy</term> <note>A tradition of esoteric philosophy and alchemy based on writings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.</note> and employs a reasonably candid style, regardless of what he chose to call himself. For the rest, there is nothing especially noteworthy to mention regarding this treatise; therefore, without further digression, we shall proceed to the text itself.

# A Conversation on the Art

In my opinion, it is most advisable to perform the <term>projection</term><note>The act of casting the alchemical medicine onto a base metal to transform it into gold or silver.</note> generally upon mercury, or in the absence of that, upon lead or tin.

**Phil.** In how much time is the projection accomplished?

**Rhom.** Provided that a good melting furnace is available, it can be sufficiently completed in one hour, or even indeed in half an hour.

**Phil.** I remember, however, that you briefly mentioned three orders above—namely the first, second, and third <term>elixirs</term><note>Refined stages of the alchemical medicine, each increasing in potency.</note>—therefore I pray you, that you would explain this to me a little more circumstantially.

**Rhom.** That which is made from the natural matter with a single straight movement (or with the first rotation of the wheel) is called the elixir of the first order. This preparation is called in the Art the "elixir of the bodies." When this is then nourished through seven <term>imbibitions</term><note>The process of adding liquid to a dry substance to saturate it without making it fluid.</note> and finally, after the last imbibition, is <term>putrefied</term><note>Subjected to a stage of decomposition or "blackness" in the vessel.</note>, made white, and <term>coagulated</term><note>Hardened or solidified from a liquid state.</note> again, it is then called the elixir of the second order. # Dialogue on the Art

->Listen not only with the ears, but also with the mind.<-

Thus, one of our species is called the principal beginning, because it introduces the determination through its effect and reduces or brings the others into its species—that is, to perfection. For this reason, in our Art, it is called the **Fire of Nature**. In the writings of Ripley <note>George Ripley (c. 1415–1490), an influential English alchemist and author of 'The Compound of Alchymie.'</note> it is called the **Mother of the Third Menstruum** <note>original: "menstrui"; in alchemy, a solvent or catalyst used to dissolve metals.</note>. This is not without cause, since this single principle determines and glorifies the other two. In this respect, the other two are called *principia superficialia* or **external beginnings**, for by them the weight is increased and the death of the *compositi* <note>the composite or combined substance</note> is brought about.

Furthermore, they also kindle the **Fire Against Nature**. Between this and the **Fire of Nature** (which lies hidden in the third principal subject of the Work), the **Unnatural Fire** or the **Middle Fire** is excited through the conjunction of both fires and the resistance of one against the other. Through its mediation, the true *putrefaction* <note>the stage of decomposition or "blackness" (nigredo) necessary for transformation</note> is fulfilled.

Thus, the subject in which the **Fire Against Nature** lies hidden is, in respect to the end goal, that principle which is most superficial or external. Of this, Pontanus <note>likely referring to the "Epistle of Pontanus," a famous alchemical text concerning the "secret fire."</note> writes that it is not transformed with the matter, although he previously sets a condition for such a fire: that it *can* be transmuted with the matter. From this, it is to be understood that of all the species, this one increases the weight of the perfect Elixir less than the others—though it does so somewhat—and from it comes primarily that which is called in the Work the *terra damnata* <note>literally "damned earth"; the useless dross or residue left after distillation or sublimation</note> or the damned...

<summary>This page explains the complex theory of the "three fires" (Natural, Against Nature, and Middle Fire) and their roles in the alchemical process of putrefaction. It cites authorities like Ripley and Pontanus to distinguish between the internal transformative principle and the external additives that result in residue.</summary>

# The Translator’s Preface.

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'O' inside a square frame decorated with floral and vine motifs.</image-desc>

ALTHOUGH the English philosopher Ripley <note>George Ripley (c. 1415–1490), a famous English alchemist and canon of Bridlington.</note> is famous throughout all Europe for his great experience and uncommon candor in the spagyric <term>spagyric: an early term for alchemy, specifically the art of separating and recombining the essential components of substances</term> writings he left behind, no one until now has set themselves to such writings to translate them into High German. This is despite the fact that many who are unskilled in the Latin and English languages—in which these works are found—have carried a great longing for them. However, since our highly celebrated Philaletha <note>Eirenaeus Philalethes, a 17th-century alchemist whose identity remains debated.</note> and his diligent disciple Starkey <note>George Starkey (1628–1665), an American-born alchemist and physician.</note> so strongly recommend and frequently cite these Ripleyan writings, and I have translated their treatises into German, I could well imagine that the German reader would also gladly wish to have Ripley’s works in German. I have therefore immediately translated his principal treatises, as many as are available, into High German and included them here, so that the reader might have both authors together. Our Ripley lived, however, at the time of the English King Edward IV, as can be seen from the letter he wrote to him; at which time also the powerful philosopher Count Bernard of Treviso <note>Bernhardus Trevisanus (1406–1490), an Italian alchemist known for his lifelong quest for the Philosopher's Stone.</note>

# Preface of the 12th Gate

You will certainly have no reason to accuse me of withholding;
I will, however, diligently instruct you,
So that you understand that there are three **Mercuries** <note>In alchemy, Mercury represents the principle of fluidity and transformation, not just the liquid metal.</note>,
Which are the keys to this science.

->13.<-

**Raymond** <note>Referring to Raymond Lully, a famous 13th-century philosopher and alchemist.</note> calls such things his **menstrua** <note>original: "menstrua"; a term for solvents or "monthly waters" used to dissolve solids into their primary matter.</note>,
Without which, in truth, nothing right is accomplished;
But among these, two are external,
While the third is of the essence of gold and
silver,
Whose properties I will soon explain to you;
And it is the essential **Mercury** of other metals,
The primary material essence of our Stone.

->14.<-

In gold and silver, our **menstrua** are not visible,
And they do not appear to the sight in deed or effect;
This is the Stone that we wish to be understood;
If one understands our writings correctly,
It is the soul, and the shining substance
Of gold and silver through their subtle influence,
Through which the earth receives its brilliance.

->15.<-

For what else are gold and silver, says **Avicenna** <note>A Persian polymath and physician whose works were foundational to medieval alchemy.</note>,
Than a pure, white, and red earth?
Take away the aforementioned brilliance from them,
And the earth will not be worth much.
The entire composite we call our lead;
The quality of the brilliance comes from the Sun and
the Moon <note>Alchemical symbols for Gold and Silver.</note>,
And these, in short, are our **menstrua**.

# Preface of the 12 Gates.

Before your gold is dissolved <note>original: "dissolviret"; the process of breaking a solid into liquid form</note>,
Let this principle be told to you above all things.

->27.<-

Now, however, I wish to divide this treatise
Into twelve chapters, with appropriate repetition,
Yet avoiding repeating what is superfluous,
And only striving to give right instruction,
As well in the theory as in the actual practice,
So that whoever allows himself to be guided by my writings
May fully achieve his undertaking.

->28.<-

The first chapter shall treat of **calcination** <note>the reduction of a substance to powder through heat</note>;
The second, of the secret Philosophical **dissolution**;
The third, of the **separation** of the elements;
The fourth, of the matrimonial **conjunction** <note>the joining of the "male" and "female" principles, often sulfur and mercury</note>;
This will be followed by the fifth, of **putrefaction** <note>the stage of decay or blackening, known as the nigredo</note>;
The sixth will be of the whitening **congealing**;
Whereupon will follow the seventh, of **cibation** <note>the "feeding" of the matter with liquid to sustain its growth</note>;

->29.<-

The eighth will show the secret of our **sublimation**;
The ninth will be of **fermentation**;
The tenth will treat briefly of **exaltation**;
The eleventh, of our mineral **multiplication**;
The twelfth, of **projection** <note>the final stage where the medicine transforms base metals into gold</note> and repetition;
And with that, this treatise shall end,
With God’s help, as I have intended.

## The First Gate: On Calcination.

-> 1. <-

Calcination <term>Calcination: the process of reducing a substance to a fine powder through heat, though here used in a specialized alchemical sense</term> is a purification of our Stone,
Which brings it back to its own natural warmth,
And loses nothing of the fundamental moisture;
It also brings our Stone to its highly necessary
solution <note>original: "solution" - the dissolving of the solid matter</note>;
But I remind you that you must follow the Philosophers,
And not go to work in the common manner,
With various prepared sulfurs and salts.

-> 2. <-

Neither with corrosives nor with fire alone,
Nor with vinegar, nor with burning waters <note>original: "brennenden Wassern" - likely referring to strong acids or distilled spirits</note>,
Nor with white lead <note>original: "Bleyrauch" - literally "lead-smoke," referring to lead acetate or ceruse</note> can our Stone
Be calcined according to our intention;
And all you who wish to calcine in such a way,
Remove your hands from this difficult science,
Until you understand our calcination better.

->3.<-

For by such <term>calcination</term> <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to powder; here, the author warns against "vulgar" calcination which destroys the essence.</note> the bodies are destroyed,
Which diminishes the moisture of our <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosophers' Stone, the ultimate goal of the alchemical work.</note>.
For when the bodies are burned to powder,
They are dried out like ashes or burnt bones.
Such a lime we do not desire at all,
For we increase the <term>radical moisture</term> <note>original: "Wurtzelfeuchtigkeit." The essential, life-giving fluid believed to exist within all matter.</note>
Through our calcining, and diminish none of it.

->4.<-

And for the foundation of our calcination,
Act cautiously, joining only like kind with like kind,
For like kind has an alluring affinity for its own kind.
Whoever does not know this is blind in the science,
And goes groping about with a darkened mind,
Ignorant of where he might encounter anything good,
Because he cannot understand our words.

->5.<-

Join kind to kind, and species to species,
For every little sprout corresponds to its own seed;
A man begets a man, a beast brings forth a beast.
Every <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritus." A volatile substance or the "soul" of the metal.</note> is <term>fixed</term> <note>original: "figiret." To make a volatile substance stable and resistant to heat.</note> with a lime of its own kind.
To treat of this more extensively is not particularly necessary,
But if you take heed of this, it will serve you well;
If you do not understand it, you are blind in the science.

We make a rich lime <term>Calx: a powder produced by heating a metal or mineral to high temperatures</term>, both white and raw,

Fluid like wax, otherwise it is of no use,

So suitable for tinting <note>original: "tingiren" - the alchemical process of changing the color and quality of a metal</note>, and so that its color remains permanent.

For therein many are deceived;
Therefore, so that you do not ruin your work,
Your bodies <note>The "bodies" refer to the solid metals used in the experiment</note> must be subtly filed,
And subtilized with an equal part of mercury,
One part gold and two parts *Luna* <note>original: "Lunæ" - the alchemical name for Silver</note>,

-> 8. <-

Then see to it that four parts of your *Mercury* <note>original: "Mercurii"</note> are to one part gold,
Two to the silver, as it is fitting to be;
And in this manner you must begin your work,
In the figure of the Holy Trinity;
Three parts of the body, and as many of the spirit,
And for the unity of the spiritual substance,
One part of the spirit more than the corporeal substance.

-> 9. <-

According to the *Repertory of Raymond* <note>original: "Raimundi Repertorio" - referring to Ramon Llull, a famous 13th-century polymath and purported alchemist</note> this is
The true proportion, for whoever wishes to look it up;

# The Second Gate

# The Third Gate.

### 2.

The Earth turns to Water in a black and dark color;
The Water thereafter becomes Air through true whiteness;

Dry out the Earth until it thirsts

And then let it drink its moisture once again.

with milk and food, gradually more and more. <note>The "child" is a common alchemical metaphor for the Philosopher's Stone in its early, volatile state; "feeding" it refers to the process of cibation, or adding liquid to the dry matter to increase its substance.</note>

-> 13. <-

For now moisture and dryness are so tempered <note>balanced</note>
that the earth has taken an <term>impression</term> <note>a lasting mark or influence</note> from the water,
and after this they can never be <term>separated</term> <note>original: "separirt"</note> from one another:
And just as the water has given the earth its entrance,
so that they now wish to dwell together steadfastly,
so the earth has shared its enduring power with the water;
therefore they are now one, and no longer <term>conflict</term> <note>original: "contrariiren"</note> with each other.

-> 14. <-

Thus our entire <term>intention</term> <note>aim or focus</note> lies in two things:
in dryness and moisture, which are two contrary things;
in the dryness which leads the moisture to <term>fixity</term> <note>the state of being non-volatile and resistant to fire</note>,
and in the moisture which introduces fluidity to the earth,
so that from these things, being so tempered, there may arise—

# The Fourth Gate.

The middle state, which is neither as thick as the body,
Nor as thin as water, is undoubtedly found there.

->15.<-

Therefore, solution and conjunction are the two principles <note>original: "principia"</note>
Of this high science, and the most prominent polar
Main-vortices;
Yet there are many more apparent principles,
Which I will explain hereafter.
Proceed therefore to another bulwark
Of this our firm castle of wisdom,
So that you may also enter through the fifth gate.

## The Fifth Gate: Of
## Putrefaction.

->1.<-

Here begins the chapter on putrefaction <note>The process of decay or "rotting" in alchemy, symbolizing the death of the old form before rebirth.</note>,
Without which neither the Solar seed nor the
Sperm is multiplied,
Which must happen solely through the continuous
Action
Of heat, and not by hands upon our body;
For without this, no body can be naturally altered,
As Christ testifies: Unless the grain of wheat
Dies in the earth, it brings forth no fruit. <note>A reference to John 12:24, a common alchemical justification for the necessity of the "death" of the matter.</note>

->2.<-

So also, unless the matter <note>original: "Materi"</note> rots,
It can by no means be altered,
Nor can the elements be naturally divided
Nor properly conjoined.

# The Fifth Gate

Therefore, so that your work does not perhaps fail,
Understand the principles of <term>putrefaction</term> <note>The process of breaking down or "rotting" the base matter to release its essence.</note> correctly
Before you begin this work.

->3.<-

Putrefaction can, according to the <term>Philosophers</term> <note>A term used by alchemists to refer to their predecessors and authorities in the "Hermetic Art."</note>, be described thus:
Namely, that it is a slaying of three bodies,
And a dividing of three things in our mixture,
Which brings the slain bodies into destruction,
And afterwards makes them fit for <term>generation</term> <note>The rebirth or creation of the new, purified substance.</note>;
For whatever is generated on Earth,
That is without doubt generated through the <term>course of the heavens</term> <note>The influence of planetary movements and celestial timing on earthly matter.</note>.

->4.<-

And therefore, as we have already considered before,
Mix your elements and balance them wisely,
And maintain them in tempered warmth, preventing above all things
That they do not become ashes through too great a heat,
Nor a dry, red, useless powder,
But rather a black powder like a <term>raven’s beak</term> <note>original: "Rabenschnabel." A traditional alchemical symbol for the "nigredo" or black stage, signifying total decomposition.</note>,
In a warm <term>bath</term> <note>original: "balneo." Referring to a water bath (bain-marie) used for gentle heating.</note> or otherwise in our <term>manure</term> <note>Decaying organic matter used as a natural, steady heat source.</note>.

->5.<-

In as much time until ninety nights have passed,
Keep them above all things in moist warmth;
Afterwards, the blackness will soon give you a sign
That they are now proceeding toward putrefaction,
Which you will nonetheless afterwards [recognize] by various colors

# The Fifth Gate

Therefore, take in the beginning our Stone <note>The "Philosopher's Stone" in its early, unrefined state.</note>
And bury each in the other’s grave,
And join them together in an equal marriage,
->together,<-
So that they lie together for six weeks and cherish
Their naturally conceived seed, and nourish and
maintain it,
And during this entire time do not rise from the grave,
A mystery which deceives many.

->10.<-

This time of conception you must await with gentle
warmth.
The appearing blackness <note>Known in alchemy as the *nigredo* stage, symbolizing death and the purging of impurities.</note> will indicate to you when
they die,
For like a liquid pitch they will at such a time
Swell and boil up, settle down again and
rot; <note>original: "erfaulen" - refers to the process of fermentation or putrefaction.</note>
Also, shining colors will appear there
Like a rainbow, quite beautiful to behold,
And then the water begins to dry out completely.

->11.<-

For when the tempered warmth acts <note>original: "agirt"</note> upon the moist
bodies,
It generates <note>original: "Generirt"</note> first of all the blackness,
Which is a certain sign of the natural conjunction <note>original: "conjunction" - the chemical and spiritual union of opposites.</note>
And of the true putrefaction <note>original: "putrefaction" - the breaking down of matter.</note>; you should not forget this,
For then you will not err regarding the perfect alteration <note>original: "alteration" - the total transformation of the substance.</note>,
And thus you must enter through the Gate of Blackness
If you wish to attain the light of Paradise in whiteness <note>original: "Weissigkeit" or *albedo*, the stage of purification following the blackness.</note>.

# The Fifth Gate

And in the whiteness of paradise, it shall be a mighty elixir.

->15.<-

And so that you may come to <term>perfection</term> <note>The final, completed state of the alchemical Stone</note> all the sooner,
Take this example as a conclusion,
For all the secrets of <term>putrefaction</term> <note>The stage of "rotting" or breaking down the matter, often called the Nigredo or blackening</note> lie hidden within it.
An oak tree that is constantly under water
Will not soon rot—believe me, as one who has experienced it—
For even if it were under water for a hundred years,
You would find it just as whole as it was at the beginning.

->16.<-

But if it is sometimes moist and sometimes dry,
As you can find by experience with other wood,
Such an oak tree will rot over time;
Therefore, conclude and know in this matter
That our tree is first scorched by the sun,
And if it is then soon cooled with water,
You can easily bring it to <term>putrefaction</term> in such a manner.

->17.<-

For being now in moisture, and now again in dryness,
Now in great heat, and now again in cold,
This causes it to quickly enter into decay,
And in such a fashion your gold shall rot in a short time;
Deal therefore with the <term>bodies</term> <note>The metallic substances or "corpses" being transformed</note> as I have told you,
And do not be too hasty with the heat during the <term>putrefaction</term>,
Lest you be forced to seek your profit afterward in the ashes.

See how one allows oneself to be taken in by this "rich" consolation;
They can boast mightily of their profits,
While carrying the name of a Philosopher alongside their gains,
As much as they are able to scrape off from a monkey's tail <note>A proverbial expression for something worthless or a deceptive trick.</note>;
Therefore, look out for yourself for God's sake, if you are wise,
That you do not incur great expenses,
For if you do, everything will only be lost.

->41.<-

These philosophers, whom I mentioned before,
Trade and chatter about many things,
Falling from one error more and more into another,
All for lack of right understanding;
For like must always have its like <note>The alchemical principle of "similia similibus," suggesting that true transformation requires a correspondence in nature which these frauds lack.</note>,
As God has ordained in all things;
O, if only they were always of such a mind!

->42.<-

Do they then expect to gather roses from a thornbush,
Or sweet apples from an elderberry tree?

# The Fifth Gate

Therefore, honest and wise people should see to it that they
->do not lose their property anymore,<-
nor hang it upon such deceivers when they encounter them,
who say, "Our Stone is trodden underfoot," <note>A common alchemical trope suggesting the prima materia is a common, lowly substance, often used by frauds to justify experimenting with filth.</note>
and for that reason, they bid one to distill base things
until their houses are full of stench.

->43.<-

Some have studied nothing at all;
should one then believe that such fellows
could be experienced philosophers? No, certainly,
->but rather fools,<-
as their works sufficiently demonstrate.
Therefore, have nothing to do with them, if you are
->wise,<-
so that they do not entice you with their caressing words
to behave according to their will.

->44.<-

Therefore, do not waste your goods uselessly,
and do not believe every chatterer,
but test, grasp, and feel everything,
and believe according to what you find.
Always guard yourself, however, against great expenses;
but if your philosopher is of a good life, <note>The author emphasizes that moral character is a prerequisite for true alchemical success.</note>
you can trust his philosophy all the better.

->45.<-

Test and examine him beforehand
concerning all the secrets of our Stone; <term>Stone: The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold and granting long life.</term>
if he does not know them, spend nothing on him,
and have nothing to do with him, but let him
->run,<-
no matter how hypocritically holy he may appear to you,
for he will commonly present himself and flatter you best
when he is most intent upon his prey.

# The Fifth Gate

### 46.

If he is able to answer you like a wise and learned man,
Even if he has not yet experienced it through experiment <note>original: "experimentiret"</note>,
It is nonetheless right to be helpful to him in his work,
Especially if he is of good character; I consider this to be just.
For he will repay it once his work succeeds;
You will also soon perceive from just a few words
Whether he has any true knowledge of our Stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold.</note>.

### 47.

There is but one thing, one vessel, and one furnace, and no more;
See whether he maintains such a principle <note>original: "principium"</note>.
If not, let him go on his way,
For he will never make you rich,
And it is indeed better to let him go now
Than later with great loss and public scrutiny,
As well as other great burdens.

### 48.

But if it is God’s will that you one day attain
This knowledge through the teachings entrusted to you,
Then reveal it to no one, no matter who they may be,
Neither for favor, nor silver, nor gold.
Be no oppressor, nor a glutton <note>original: "Pancketirer" - one who wastes wealth on lavish banquets</note>, nor a boaster,
But serve God, and let the poor be commended to your care,
So long as you wish to live long upon the earth.

### 49.

Keep your secrets always to yourself;
Reveal them to no wicked men who do not fear God,
Lest they perhaps cast you into prison
Until you teach them so that they can do it too.

### The Sixth Gate of
#### Congelation.

->1.<-

It is a hardening of soft things into a white

# The Sixth Gate

->2.<-

But there occur in certain ways the <term>congealings</term><note>original: "congelirungen"; the process of turning a liquid into a solid or stable state</note>
Of the <term>Spirits and Bodies</term><note>In alchemy, "Spirits" usually refer to volatile substances like mercury or sulfur, while "Bodies" refer to solid metals</note> which have been dissolved into clear water,
As also of the <term>salts</term><note>original: "salien"</note> which are dissolved two or three times,
And congealed again into a fluid matter;
Of which congealings the fools make much talk,
And some dissolve and divide the <term>Elements</term> with their hands,
And afterwards congeal them into a dry powder.

->3.<-

But such a congealing we do not seek at all,
For it is altogether contrary to our <term>Work</term><note>The "Great Work" or "Opus Magnum," the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</note>;
For our congealing does not fear the fire,
As it must always remain steadfast therein,
And be rich with a very beautiful <term>tincture</term><note>The "tincture" is the transformative essence or color that allows the Stone to transmute base metals into gold</note>,
Which congealed thing does not melt away in the air
Into water; for in such a manner our Work would be spoiled.

->4.<-

Therefore it is not congealed into such a hard stone,
Like glass or crystal, which flow from violent fire,
But rather it melts quickly like a wax,
Without the blowing of the bellows; and see that you are not deceived,
For such a congealing is not suited to our purpose,
Which turns to water, like the congealed salts,
But rather one that melts and yet remains permanent.

# The Sixth Gate

And once you congeal <note>original: "congelireſt"; the process of turning a liquid into a solid state</note> it into the Whiteness,

-> 8. <-

And just as the dry was putrefied <note>original: "putreficiret"; the stage of decomposition or "the crow's head"</note> by the moist,

Just as in the blackness the moisture shows itself
With many and various new, ever-changing colors.

-> 9. <-

The cause of all this is the very tempered heat,

Not as the fools do in a Sophistical <note>A derogatory term for "false" alchemists who only sought to imitate the appearance of gold rather than achieve true transformation</note> manner according to outward appearance,
But in such a way that all parts withstand every fire,
Fluid, fixed, and constant in the tincture <note>original: "tinctur"; the potent substance capable of transmuting base metals</note>.

-> 10. <-

The art of medicine <note>original: "Arzneykunſt"</note> also gives an account of such digestion <note>The alchemical process of slow, consistent heating, likened to the biological process of breaking down food</note>,

It produces, without contradiction, the Whiteness,
Just as the second digestion causes the Redness <note>original: "Röhte"; the final stage of the Great Work, known as the Rubedo</note>,

# The Sixth Gate.

# The Sixth Gate

And keep in your mind the aforementioned proportion <note>The specific ratios of materials required for the alchemical mixture</note>;
